articles.title: Is Iran plotting a ‘dirty bomb’ attack in the US? What we know
articles.summary: A CNN report quoting unnamed US officials alleges Tehran is developing plans for an attack on officials in Washington.
articles.body:
CNN has reported that United States intelligence indicates Iran is developing plans to target senior officials in President Donald Trump’s administration with a “dirty bomb” or a chemical weapon in Washington, DC. The broadcaster quotes seven unnamed US officials.

However, the report sets out no evidence to support the claims.

According to CNN, its sources described the planning as an effort by Tehran to give itself options, not as an imminent attack. One source said US intelligence had picked up Iranian “chatter” indicating that bomb-making materials had been stashed inside the US. That claim has not been independently verified.

The White House said it was “monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time, there are no credible threats to the homeland”. Iran’s mission to the United Nations said Tehran “categorically rejects and unequivocally refutes the false and fabricated allegations”.

The report was released as talks to end the US-Israel war on Iran have stalled and Trump said last week that Washington does not “need” a deal. The aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt has just arrived in the region, bringing the number of US carriers there to three and adding to fears of a renewed escalation.

So what is a dirty bomb? Could Iran build one? And how seriously should the latest claims be taken?

A dirty bomb, technically known as a radiological dispersal device, combines conventional explosives, such as dynamite, with radioactive material. When the bomb explodes, the resulting blast scatters the radioactive material into the surrounding area.

Unlike a nuclear weapon, a dirty bomb does not need enriched uranium or a nuclear chain reaction. The radioactive material can come from medical or industrial equipment, such as machines used in hospitals and research facilities. That makes a dirty bomb far cheaper and easier to build than a nuclear device. It is also far less destructive.

The main health risk comes from breathing in contaminated dust near the blast. As the material spreads, it becomes less concentrated and less harmful. The damage depends on the size of the explosive charge, the type and amount of radioactive material and the weather, especially the wind.

According to the US National Academy of Sciences, most dirty bombs would immediately contaminate an area of one or two city blocks although wind could carry radioactive particles over a few square miles.

Experts said dirty bombs are unlikely to cause mass casualties. In testimony to the US Senate in 2002, Richard Meserve, then-chairman of the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission, estimated that deaths in most scenarios would be in the tens, not the hundreds or thousands.

“It’s important to understand that a dirty bomb isn’t an off-the-shelf nuclear bomb. There aren’t any mushroom clouds and massive shockwaves tearing down buildings and killing hundreds of thousands of people in the blink of an eye,” Talha Abdulrazaq, a researcher at the University of Exeter’s Strategy and Security Institute told Al Jazeera. “Instead, its primary effect would be psychological panic and hysteria in the target state alongside radioactive contamination, turning the area hit into a no-go zone.”

That is why experts call dirty bombs “weapons of mass disruption” rather than weapons of mass destruction.

Does Iran have the ability to build one?

In theory, yes. But so do many states and armed groups.

A dirty bomb is “really easy to make”, Scott Roecker, vice president for nuclear materials security at the Nuclear Threat Initiative, told Al Jazeera in 2022. Radioactive sources used in medicine and industry can be found in many countries and building a crude device does not require advanced technical knowledge.

Iran has a large civilian nuclear programme. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency’s last assessment, it held about 440kg (970lb) of uranium enriched to 60 percent as of June 2025.

In an April analysis for the European Council on Foreign Relations, Jacek Siewiera, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, wrote that although the stockpile falls short of what is needed for a nuclear weapon, it “could be extraordinarily dangerous from a radiological and sabotage perspective”. He warned that a dirty bomb could be “either a deliberate element of escalation or an unintended consequence of weakened central control” because international institutions no longer know who controls Iran’s nuclear storage sites.

But even enriched uranium is only weakly radioactive, which makes it a poor choice for a dirty bomb. Many analysts also argued that Tehran would be unlikely to waste material it spent decades producing.

A June 2025 analysis by Chris Kremidas-Courtney for the Euro-Atlantic Resilience Centre, a Bucharest-based think tank, reached a similar conclusion.

Iran is “widely believed to have access to sufficient radioactive material for use in dirty bombs, particularly from civilian nuclear and industrial sources”, he wrote. He pointed to isotopes such as caesium-137, used in cancer treatment, and cobalt-60, used in industrial radiography.

Kremidas-Courtney, however, described a dirty bomb as a possible “tool of last resort under extreme circumstances”. He also judged that the US “poses a high bar for direct infiltration” and ports and maritime chokepoints, such as the Strait of Hormuz, were more plausible targets.

Building a dirty bomb “is actually far easier than a conventional nuclear weapon” and does not require highly enriched uranium, Abdulrazaq said. Even after US strikes on the Fordow and Natanz nuclear facilities, “a degraded capability doesn’t mean a destroyed capability,” he told Al Jazeera. “Iran certainly has access to all the components and expertise required to construct something as rudimentary as a dirty bomb.”

Iran “doesn’t have the missile or drone capability to strike US targets 10,000km [6,200 miles] and more away”, Abdulrazaq said. Therefore, any attack on Washington, DC, would almost certainly rely on clandestine smuggling networks or links to organised crime.

Even if Iran has the technical means, there is little public evidence that it has any ambition to build a dirty bomb, let alone set one off on US soil. Abdulrazaq said using a radiological weapon “would instantly destroy Iran’s remaining diplomatic credit” and would likely lead to an invasion and the collapse of its government.

“I highly doubt Iranian strategists are unaware of this reality, so the likelihood of a dirty bomb remains infinitesimally remote.”

According to CNN’s sources, US officials are divided on this point. One source said officials were debating whether Iran even had the personnel in place to carry out such an attack. The report also said there is no evidence that Tehran has decided to go ahead.

Iran does have a record of plotting against US officials. US prosecutors charged an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps operative in 2024 over an alleged murder-for-hire plot against Trump. But CNN noted that such plotting has mostly focused on opportunities to target officials while they travel abroad.

The latest report followed a series of US media stories about alleged Iranian plots. In October, the Axios news website and The New York Times reported on a memo from the director of national intelligence warning that Iranian plots against US personnel abroad had reached “advanced stages”. One official said some Iranian operatives may already be active inside the US. The memo did not identify specific targets or methods.

Critics said such reports, which often quote anonymous officials, risk building public support for escalation at a time when the war is deeply unpopular. In October, a Chicago Council on Global Affairs survey found that nearly 70 percent of respondents said the war was not worth fighting.

Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei dismissed the CNN report as baseless. In a post on X, he suggested the claims were meant to frighten the public and build support for further hostile action against Iran.

Abdulrazaq noted that the claims came from “a US intelligence assessment rather than a direct threat made by Tehran”. “The Iraq war in 2003 and the lies surrounding Iraqi WMDs [weapons of mass destruction] is sufficient enough to doubt publicly communicated intelligence assessments in a wartime information environment,” he said.

He added that a dirty bomb attack would “hand-deliver the political rationale” for a major US war on Iran, including a ground invasion, with bipartisan support even after Democrats take control of Congress in January. “Iranian strategists aren’t stupid, and if I’m telling you this, they surely have made similar assessments, so I highly doubt the veracity of these intelligence reports,” he said.

Has the US gone to war on faulty intelligence before?

Before the 2003 invasion, President George W Bush’s administration argued that Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein had weapons of mass destruction and links to al-Qaeda. In February 2003, Secretary of State Colin Powell made the US government’s case to the United Nations Security Council, including claims that Iraq had mobile biological weapons laboratories.

No stockpiles were found after the US-led invasion was carried out. In 2005, a presidential commission concluded that US intelligence on Iraq’s weapons had been “dead wrong”. Much of the case rested on unreliable sources, including an Iraqi defector codenamed “Curveball”, whose claims about mobile labs proved to be fabricated.

The media also came under scrutiny. In 2004, The New York Times published an editors’ note acknowledging that some of its pre-war coverage, much of it based on unnamed officials and Iraqi exiles, had not been as rigorous as it should have been.

Four decades earlier, two reported attacks on US destroyers in the Gulf of Tonkin that the US government had said were unprovoked were used to justify a major US escalation in Vietnam. However, North Vietnam carried out the first attack in 1964 after US raids on its coast, and later evidence showed the second reported North Vietnamese attack two days later most likely never happened.

No successful dirty bomb attack has ever been recorded.

In 1995, Chechen fighters planted a container of radioactive caesium in Moscow’s Izmailovsky Park, but it never detonated. In 1998, a container of radioactive material rigged with explosives was discovered and defused near a railway line in Chechnya.

There have been other scares. In 2002, US authorities arrested Jose Padilla, an American accused of plotting a dirty bomb attack though he was never charged. In 2013, a truck carrying radioactive cobalt-60 from a hospital was stolen in Mexico, prompting UN warnings that the material could be used in a dirty bomb.

In 2022, Russia accused Ukraine of preparing to set off a dirty bomb and blame Moscow. Western governments dismissed the claim as “transparently false”.

articles.title: Houthi advance on Aden may spur resurgence of Yemen’s southern separatists
articles.summary: Southern separatists try to regain power to defend Aden as Saudi Arabia reshuffles its military command against Houthis.
articles.body:
A looming Houthi military threat to the Yemeni government’s de facto capital of Aden has increased the importance of the Southern Transitional Council (STC), a southern secessionist movement, analysts have said.

The STC, which is believed to be supported by the United Arab Emirates, seeks an independent state for southern Yemen. An announcement that it had disbanded was made at the start of the year, following a Saudi-backed military campaign by Yemeni government forces against it. Other STC senior members declared the dissolution “null and void”, but the group had remained weakened in the months since.

However, following the sudden withdrawal of forces aligned with the internationally recognised Yemeni government from key positions on Yemen’s Red Sea coast this week, southern separatists now appear poised to gain more influence in the south.

With the Houthi group, also known as Ansar Allah, now 60km (37 miles) from the southern city, factions linked to the STC have stepped up to defend Aden from the Houthi advance.

Amr al-Bidh, a special representative for the STC president, has blamed the collapse of government forces on Yemen’s Red Sea coast in September, as well as recent Houthi gains, on the government campaign against the southern separatists earlier this year.

“In January, the most effective anti-Houthi force in Yemen was taken apart by decisions in Riyadh, not by the Houthis,” al-Bidh told Al Jazeera.

STC leader Aidarous al-Zubaidi , who is believed to be based in the UAE and has maintained his distance from the Yemeni government, recently launched a mobilisation campaign across the south to prepare for the defence of Aden, Lahij and al-Dhalea.

Al-Bidh said that for the STC to stop the Houthi advance, it would require autonomy on the battlefield for its units.

“No front can be held for long when the people defending it have no say in how it is defended. What’s missing is a political decision to let southerners lead their own defence. We’re ready to put every capacity we have towards defending Aden,” al-Bidh said.

“We’ve always said the war will only end with a political solution that deals with the root of the conflict. That includes the right of the southern people to decide their own future. What won’t work is a deal made over the heads of southerners and signed by people who don’t represent them.”

Abdy Yeganeh, policy director for Independent Diplomat, said the STC could serve as a major bulwark against the Houthis during their current offensive.

“As a result of the January fallout between Saudi Arabia and the STC, the STC forces were weakened and undermined,” Yeganeh told Al Jazeera.

“Events in recent weeks have shown that despite attempts of marginalising the STC, they remain a credible local entity with significant popular support, with tens of thousands marching weekly across the south in their favour and with a capable military.”

But military and strategic affairs expert Ali al-Dahab said that the STC remains politically divided and sections have become highly dependent on Saudi financial support.

“Without the support of the government and the support of Saudi Arabia, it cannot [repel the Houthis],” al-Dahab told Al Jazeera. “The capabilities of the Houthis have exceeded the combined capabilities of the government, let alone the [Southern] Transitional Council.”

The STC and Yemeni government forces have fought together against the Houthis, who captured Sanaa in September 2014. But relations between the two sides have also been fraught with differences, including clashes for control of positions and facilities in Aden and southern Yemen.

Following STC advances in southern Yemen in December 2025, the Saudi-led coalition, which has militarily supported the Yemeni government since March 2015, launched air strikes on an alleged UAE-linked weapons shipment to southern separatists. Al-Zubaidi fled Yemen, and some STC units came under the command of Saudi-backed forces. One of the most powerful forces affiliated with it, the Southern Giants Brigades , is now aligned with Saudi Arabia.

Saudi Arabia’s King Salman issued a royal decree on Monday replacing Lieutenant General Fahd bin Hamad al-Salman with General Fayyad al-Ruwaili as the commander of its forces fighting the Houthis.

Al-Dahab said that appointing al-Ruwaili, Saudi Arabia’s chief of the general staff, to this role centralises decision-making in the face of a Houthi offensive.

“It gives the position greater power because whoever will assume command of the joint forces is the Saudi Chief of Staff,” al-Dahab said.

articles.title: After working on an auto assembly line, Berry Gordy borrowed $800 from his family’s co-op in 1959 to start a record business; it grew into Motown, a force in American music
articles.summary: Discover the inspiring story of Berry Gordy, who transformed an $800 loan into Motown Records, shaping the landscape of American music with iconic artists like Marvin Gaye and Diana Ross.
articles.body: Many could easily hum their favourite songs by Marvin Gaye, Stevie Wonder and The Temptations. Yet few would recognise the man behind the label that made them quintessential to American music. Berry Gordy was a trailblazer with hustle. According to the National Portrait Gallery, before he founded a cornerstone of the music industry, Gordy worked in a boxing ring, ran a record shop, and fitted upholstery on a car assembly line.In 1959, he borrowed $800 from his family co-operative and started a record business in Detroit. Gordy was born in 1929, the seventh of eight children of Berry Gordy Sr. and Bertha Fuller Gordy. He left school in the 11th grade and tried his shot at the life of a pugilist before he settled on songwriting. Military service interrupted his work: he was drafted in 1951 and served in the Korean War. Once he returned, he opened a jazz records shop, which unfortunately closed down not long after. He then took a job at a Lincoln-Mercury plant and concurrently wrote songs.From a Detroit flat to a hit-making record labelGordy bought the property at 2648 West Grand Boulevard and moved his wife and young son into the upper flat. The record label operated from the ground floor. Studio A was converted from a rear photography studio and became a recording space. Gordy named the building Hitsville U.S.A.According to Motown Museum, the record company was incorporated in April 1960. In 1959, Barrett Strong released “Money (That’s What I Want), for which Gordy, alongside Janie Bradford, was credited as a songwriter. The Miracles later released “Shop Around”, written by Smokey Robinson. It reached number one on the national R&B chart and number two on the Billboard pop chart. Gordy also wrote or co-wrote other songs by Jackie Wilson, including “Reet Petite”, “Lonely Teardrops” and “To Be Loved”.Besides his flair for songwriting, Gordy also had an eye for talent, and his early discoveries included the Matadors, who became the Miracles, Mary Wells, the Marvelettes, and the Primes and Primettes, later named the Temptations and the Supremes. The National Portrait Gallery also lists the Four Tops, Martha Reeves and the Vandellas, Marvin Gaye, Tammi Terrell and the Jackson 5 among the artists he brought to the mainstream. Gordy actively participated in preparing them for public appearances. Motown’s artist-development staff worked with singers on posture, speech and conduct. Coordinated clothing and choreography gave groups a consistent stage presentation. Gordy also famously changed some performers’ names, including Little Stevie Wonder, born Stevland Hardway Morris.In one account, recorded by the National Portrait Gallery, he once called the Miracles to the studio at 3 am to record “Shop Around” again. He wanted artists to gauge songs by themselves by imagining a situation where they would either spend a dollar on a record or a hot dog. The question put the commercial test plainly: would this song be a hit?Hollywood lights and a bittersweet endingBy the late 1960s, Gordy had set his sights on newer landscapes: towards Los Angeles and the film and television industries. He moved Motown from Detroit to Los Angeles in 1972. As per the National Portrait Gallery, the move was followed by the departure of acts including the Jackson 5 and the Temptations.Subsequently, Gordy began producing films. Billy Dee Williams starred opposite Diana Ross in “Lady Sings the Blues” and “Mahogany”. Diana Ross and Michael Jackson later appeared in “The Wiz”, the screen version of the Broadway musical. The projects brought Motown artists into the spotlight of cinema, while Gordy produced the movies.Around the middle of the 1980s, Motown Industries was losing money, according to the National Portrait Gallery. Consequently, Gordy sold Motown to MCA in 1988. The same year he entered the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. The Motown Museum noted he had earlier moved from the company’s leading role to board chairman, and gave younger executives the opportunity to run it. The sale ended his ownership of the record label he started.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: York City player pleads not guilty over alleged punch of Rochdale fan
articles.summary: Hiram Boateng has pleaded not guilty to a public order charge at Manchester Magistrates' Court.
articles.body:
A York City FC player has appeared in court after allegedly punching a Rochdale AFC supporter during a pitch invasion.

Hiram Boateng, 30, of Leeds, pleaded not guilty at Manchester Magistrates' Court on Monday to using threatening, abusive or insulting behaviour with intent to cause fear of, or provoke, unlawful violence.

The charge relates to an incident involving fans who entered the pitch during the final-day match between the two sides at the Crown Oil Arena on 25 April.

York City FC said it was "aware of developments" following the incident and added Boateng, whose trial is due to begin on 23 June 2027, "maintains the full support of everyone at York City".

Rochdale supporters entered the pitch during the match after believing their side had secured the National League title. The alleged incident happened during a second pitch invasion later in the game, after a late goal instead gave the title to York.

A spokesperson for York City FC said: "We are aware of developments regarding the incident involving Hiram Boateng during the game against Rochdale in April.

"We are continuing to work with him and all the appropriate authorities to address this and to understand the circumstances that led to this.

"Hiram maintains the full support of everyone at York City and is a much-valued member of the squad, both on and off the pitch."

Boateng is charged with a Section 4 public order offence which carries a maximum sentence of six months in prison.

articles.title: US officially loses measles-free status after 26 years in historic setback
articles.summary: A major health organisation declared measles endemic in US for first time since 2000, reversing decades of progress.
articles.body:
The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, reversing a public health achievement maintained for 26 years, as the country grapples with its largest outbreak in more than three decades.

The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) , the Americas branch of the World Health Organization (WHO), declared measles endemic in the US, Bolivia and Mexico on Tuesday after determining that the same strain of the virus had circulated continuously in each country for at least 12 months.

An international panel of experts that advises PAHO on the prevalence of measles and rubella “recommended that the measles elimination status be withdrawn”, said Dr Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO, “a recommendation which I have accepted”.

Measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000.

Countries that lost their measles elimination status are required to submit a corrective action plan to PAHO in the coming weeks. PAHO said it will submit its recommendations to the countries in the next few days.

PAHO’s announcement follows a review of epidemiological and laboratory evidence submitted by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

In a joint statement issued on Tuesday, the CDC said it remained committed to stopping measles outbreaks and regaining the country’s elimination status.

“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” CDC Director Erica Schwartz said, adding that the agency would continue working to contain outbreaks.

The CDC said it has provided approximately $100m in additional funding to state and local health departments since August to strengthen vaccination efforts, surveillance and outbreak response.

The US has recorded approximately 7,700 measles infections since the beginning of 2025, according to CDC figures.

It is the highest number of cases the country has seen in more than 30 years. The climbing numbers come as vaccine hesitancy has grown under Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has repeatedly cast doubt on the safety of vaccines despite scientific evidence to the contrary.

Before taking office, Kennedy claimed that no vaccine was “safe and effective” and promoted the discredited theory that vaccines cause autism.

To protect against illness, children are commonly given the measles vaccine in a combined shot with mumps and rubella vaccines, known by the acronym MMR.

But the vaccination rate among preschoolers in the US has fallen to about 92 percent, below the level experts say is needed to prevent major outbreaks.

As health secretary under US President Donald Trump, Kennedy has questioned the MMR vaccine’s ability to protect children.

He has suggested that the MMR vaccine’s effectiveness wanes by about 4.5 percent a year and said it contains “aborted fetus debris”, a claim experts have rejected as false .

The CDC has confirmed six measles-related deaths this year, but state health officials in Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and New York have reported 10 deaths combined, a discrepancy that has fuelled tensions between federal and state health authorities over how measles deaths are classified and counted.

Measles is considered highly infectious, and the WHO estimates the virus caused 95,000 deaths worldwide in 2024, mostly among children.

Matt Ferrari, a biology professor and director of Pennsylvania State University’s Center for Infectious Disease Dynamics, believes the loss of the US’s measles elimination status can serve as a wake-up call for public health officials.

“This should be a humbling statement for the United States,” Ferrari told Al Jazeera.

For much of his career, Ferrari has studied strategies to control measles in countries around the world. The US was previously seen as a model.

“It was a motivating achievement that we use to drive support for measles elimination programmes all around the world,” said Ferrari. “Now we need to be looking for expertise elsewhere because we haven’t been pulling our weight.”

Edwin Asturias, a professor of paediatrics, infectious disease and epidemiology at the University of Colorado, described the loss of status as a “stain” on the country’s public health programme.

“Measles cases are a signal that your immunisation programme and other systems within your public health services are having problems,” he told Al Jazeera.

Asturias said the US had the resources and experience to prevent the resurgence of the virus, pointing to its success in eliminating local measles transmission for more than a quarter of a century.

About 40 percent of current US measles cases are among adults older than 20, he said, highlighting the need to expand vaccination efforts.

Reaching these populations will require making vaccines available in workplaces, places of worship and other community settings, rather than relying solely on paediatricians and family doctors, Asturias explained.

The loss of elimination status also has implications beyond US borders , as measles can spread through international travel and migration.

“The United States is not, any more, a place where you’re safe from measles,” Asturias told Al Jazeera. “If you’re a common person walking around with your children, you need to know now that measles has come to the country to stay unless something else is done.”

The risk is particularly concerning for unvaccinated people and those who cannot receive the vaccine, including those with weakened immune systems or people undergoing cancer treatment.

Public health experts say the announcement should serve as a catalyst for a more extensive vaccination response.

While they do not expect PAHO’s announcement to prompt a significant change in federal policy, some hope it will spur action among state and local health departments.

Ferrari argued that the US should look to countries with experience containing measles outbreaks, including India, where community health workers visit households to identify children who may have missed vaccinations or whose families may be reluctant to vaccinate.

He also suggested that states may need to reconsider vaccination strategies, including whether to offer an earlier first or second dose to protect young children in areas where measles is circulating.

In the US, children are routinely given two doses of the MMR vaccine. The first dose is typically administered to children at 12 to 15 months of age and the second at four to six years, before they start school. Two doses are about 97 percent effective at preventing measles.

In countries where measles transmission is more widespread, the second MMR dose is often given between the ages of 18 and 24 months.

In June, Pennsylvania began recommending an additional early dose, called a “dose zero”, for infants aged six months and older in areas with sustained measles transmission. Ferrari said this was a perfect example of how states could adapt their approaches locally.

But the prospect of a broader shift in the federal response remains unlikely.

CDC Director Schwartz said last week the agency would continue “doing the same exact thing” in terms of its measles response if the US lost its elimination status.

For Asturias, the federal response so far raises concerns about whether the country has the public health leadership needed to reverse the outbreak.

“This is hard to see happen,” he said. “But at the same time, it is predictable when you don’t have experts running a public healthcare system.”

articles.title: In November 2026, model Bella Hadid donated $50,000 toward winter shelter kits for 100 displaced families in Gaza, including waterproof tents, mattresses and blankets, after heavy rain worsened conditions
articles.summary: Model Bella Hadid has donated $50,000 to Tents of Hope’s Winter Tent Kits for Gaza initiative, providing emergency shelter supplies for 100 displaced
articles.body: Model Bella Hadid has donated $50,000 to Tents of Hope’s Winter Tent Kits for Gaza initiative, providing emergency shelter supplies for 100 displaced families as winter conditions worsen in Gaza. The donation, announced in an Instagram post and reported by Arab News and Roya News, will fund waterproof tents, blankets, and mattresses for families living in makeshift shelters.Hadid’s post came after heavy rain and flooding worsened conditions for families already displaced from their homes. She described the shelter crisis as urgent, saying that for hundreds of thousands of people, a worn out tent is the only barrier between them and the cold.What the donation coversThe $50,000 gift is enough to provide 100 complete family shelter kits. Each kit includes a waterproof tent, blankets, and mattresses, offering basic protection from rain, cold, and exposure. Hadid also broke down the cost of individual items to encourage others to give. She said $25 could provide a blanket, $30 a mattress, $75 could waterproof a tent, and $250 could fund an entire tent.Her message stressed that even smaller donations could help. She urged followers to share the appeal and contribute whatever they could, saying that every contribution matters when families are facing hypothermia and other winter dangers.Why the timing mattersWinter has arrived in Gaza, and heavy rain has made already difficult conditions worse. Hadid’s post included an illustration reading that more than 70,000 tents had been destroyed by flooding.Roya News reported that a winter storm earlier in the month flooded the tents and shelters of around 26,000 households. At the same time, aid groups had only about 2,800 tents available against an estimated need of 121,000.Hadid highlighted aid groups’ estimate that Gaza needs at least 300,000 tents to provide basic shelter for displaced families. She argued that the scale of the crisis should not obscure the individual families struggling to survive the winter.A call to actionHadid used her platform not only to announce her donation but to encourage others to act. She said she was not sharing the number for its own sake, but because she believes the gap can close one family at a time if enough people contribute.Her appeal focused on practical support rather than broad statements. By explaining exactly what different amounts could buy, she gave followers a clear sense of how their money could translate into shelter, warmth, and protection. She also emphasised that families need more than temporary shelter. Hadid argued that Palestinians have the right to live safely and with dignity, not just to survive in tents.Hadid’s ongoing advocacyThe donation builds on Hadid’s long standing public support for Palestinian rights. The Palestinian American model has repeatedly used her platform to highlight displacement and suffering, including her family’s history during the 1948 Nakba.In June 2024, Bella and her sister Gigi Hadid donated a combined $1 million to four organisations supporting Palestinians: Heal Palestine, the Palestine Children’s Relief Fund, World Central Kitchen, and UNRWA. Hadid has also spoken about the personal cost of her activism. In a 2022 interview, she said her outspoken support for Palestine had cost her modelling opportunities and friendships, but she said she would not stop speaking about her family’s history and Palestinian rights.A humanitarian crisis in focusThe latest appeal comes as Gaza faces another winter amid widespread displacement and a severe shortage of shelter. The International Rescue Committee has warned that restrictions on bringing shelter materials into Gaza are worsening the crisis.Hadid’s donation provides immediate help for 100 families, but the broader need remains enormous. With hundreds of thousands of people relying on tents for protection, aid groups say the gap between available supplies and actual demand is still wide.For the families receiving the kits, the impact is immediate. A waterproof tent, blankets, and mattresses can make the difference between enduring a cold, wet night and facing serious health risks.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Jensen Huang says he would be 'honoured' to return as Nvidia CEO if board asked him
articles.summary: Huang says he has had an "outpouring" of calls from investors and others calling for him to return.
articles.body:
Jensen Huang said he would be "honoured" to return as the boss of tech giant Nvidia if the board asked him to, in his first public comments since his shock resignation.

"I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely," Huang said on X, days after reports he had extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy.

He said he had an "outpouring" of calls from company employees, investors and others calling for him to return as CEO of Nvidia.

But, as the BBC reported on Monday, Nvidia's board is not considering bringing him back to lead the company.

The prospect of Huang returning at this point looks unlikely.

The company's board is investigating his conduct , which includes an alleged affair with an Nvidia executive.

The AI chip giant is set to report its financial results later on Tuesday, during which the company's interim chief executive, Collette Kress, may address the situation with Huang.

Beyond the internal Nvidia investigation, Huang's affair with a woman suspected of being an asset for Beijing is set to see the billionaire questioned before multiple committees of US lawmakers in the weeks ahead.

The Nvidia founder said he had "made serious mistakes in my personal life".

Nonetheless, Huang's statement appeared to show some hope he would be able to move past the major corporate scandal.

Huang said people have continued to "reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics".

"If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang added.

Many technology executives in recent days have praised Huang's role in the artificial intelligence boom. A petition began circulating online over the weekend calling for his reinstatement at the company.

Yet, by Monday, many executives were not openly calling for Huang's return.

Brad Gerstner, a major tech investor who knows Huang personally and also holds a significant stake in Nvidia, last week wrote an open letter saying that Nvidia could consider Huang's reinstatement.

On Monday, Gerstner said during an event hosted by Semafor that his letter had been misunderstood and the investigation into Huang's conduct needed to run its course.

While Gerstner questioned the facts around Huang's departure, he added: "I don't know to what degree he misled the board. If I was on a board I would take that very seriously. Let's be clear no one is above the law."

articles.title: Biden accuses Pelosi of working 'furiously' behind scenes to derail his 2024 campaign
articles.summary: Joe Biden's new book claims Nancy Pelosi worked behind the scenes to get his delegates to defect, though she has denied playing a role in any pressure campaign.
articles.body: Former President Joe Biden wrote in his new book published Tuesday that former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi worked "furiously" behind the scenes to get elected officials and Biden delegates to abandon him in 2024, though Pelosi has denied leading a pressure campaign. "That same morning, after an appearance on Morning Joe, Nancy Pelosi came to see me privately in the White House. She had been a great friend through the years. I admired her skill as Speaker and as a legislative leader. I always saw her as the political operator who learned the trade from her father, Tommy D'Alesandro, the former mayor of Baltimore, as opposed to the wealthy, liberal San Francisco Democrat caricatured in the Republican attack machine," Biden wrote. Pelosi, in July 2024, following Biden's disastrous debate performance, said during an interview on "Morning Joe," "It’s up to the president to decide if he is going to run." The remarks suggested Biden was still weighing his options despite his insistence at the time that he would remain in the race. HILLARY CLINTON HAMMERS JOE BIDEN FOR 2024 REELECTION BID DESPITE SUPPORTING CAMPAIGN: 'TERRIBLE MISTAKE' "Now, she was making a 'strategic reassessment.' Publicly she was still saying it was my decision to make. But privately she was working furiously behind the scenes to get elected officials and Biden delegates to defect," the former president wrote of Pelosi. Biden's book, "Promise Me, America," was published Tuesday and details his decision to exit the 2024 presidential race, as well as his reasons for seeking a second term, among other topics. JOE BIDEN SAYS CANCER SLOWED HIM DOWN, LIMITING MEMOIR PROMOTION TOUR The former president said Pelosi had heaped praise on him during their July 2024 meeting but sounded the alarm on the polling. "Then she told me how terrible my polling was and that I would be dragging her most vulnerable members down. She told me all the polling she had seen said I couldn't win, but I could be the George Washington of our time if I passed the torch," he wrote. EX-BIDEN STAFFER BLAMES BIDEN'S 'HUBRIS' FOR THE 'HELLSCAPE THAT WE LIVE IN': REPORT Biden wrote that Pelosi asked him to call one of his senior advisors, Mike Donilon, to go over the polling. "I told her I trusted Mike. That he had been with me for forty years. And he had been right in 2016 and 2020 and 2022 when so many of the pollsters had gotten it wrong. Mike walked her through the numbers, making the case that the race was close and still winnable. She didn't buy any of it. She told me that I wasn't getting an honest assessment of where the race stood. She was blunt: There were no polls that said I had any chance to win," Biden wrote. JILL BIDEN ADMITS PRESIDENT BIDEN WOULD NOT HAVE BEEN ABLE TO SERVE ANOTHER FOUR YEARS Biden ultimately dropped out of the race on July 21, 2024. He maintained in his book that he believed he was the best person to run against President Donald Trump, who defeated former Vice President Kamala Harris after she replaced Biden at the top of the Democratic ticket. articles.title: A Kremlin trap? Europe sees danger in Vladimir Putin’s new demand in U.S. talks
articles.summary: European leaders have long feared being frozen out of U.S.-Russia peace talks about Ukraine. Now  Trump’s team negotiating the continent’s security structure.
articles.body: LONDON — When European nations said they wanted greater involvement in Ukraine peace talks, this was almost certainly not what they had in mind. Europe has long demanded more say in negotiations to end Russia’s war, fearful of being frozen out by Washington and Moscow. They dread a deal favorable to President Vladimir Putin — who will meet President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a historic three-way meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday. The good news for them is that the United States says it is now pushing to include Europe in the next rounds of diplomacy. The bad news, say governments, officials and foreign policy analysts, is the alarming new suggestion from Trump’s team: that the entire future of European security should be up for discussion too — the same demand that Putin has pushed for years. To the Russian leader, redrawing Europe’s security map means scaling back NATO’s presence, righting what he perceives as the injustices imposed on Moscow after the Soviet Union’s collapse. A succession of senior European officials have lambasted the idea, warning that Washington risks “walking into Moscow’s trap,” as Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s foreign policy chief, put it. “This is all rather bizarre,” former Estonian President Toomas Hendrik Ilves said, summing up this sentiment in an interview with NBC News on Monday. It’s not clear how or why the U.S. came to float a maximalist demand that Putin first made in 2021, one that was widely rejected by Western governments months before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. But in recent days, as Washington ups its pressure for a breakthrough in peace talks, Russia and the U.S. have both revived the idea. Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law and envoy, wrote Friday that talks should tackle the “broader postwar European security arrangements.” Earlier this month, he lamented “decades of mistrust” and “competing security concerns” between Russia and Europe, vowing to address these by building an “enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.” Kushner has also stressed that NATO would remain central to European defense and that no country should have a veto over another’s alliances. Trump himself has also hinted that he seeks a final deal encompassing the entire continent. “It’s going to be a big agreement and it’s going to involve more than Ukraine,” he told reporters in the Oval Office earlier this month. “I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It’s going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone’s going to be thrilled.” Instead, the idea has been met with unease and dismay, viewed by many in Europe as echoing Putin’s hard-line war goals. Whereas Kushner described Europe and Russia as neighbors unable to resolve their differences, the historical record shows the aggression has chiefly been directed one way. Russia seized Ukraine’s Crimean Peninsula in 2014, then launching a full-scale invasion in 2022, while waging sabotage, cyberattacks and disinformation against the West. Kushner’s suggestion also touches on a central European fear: that Washington will pursue a deal at almost any cost, even if that emboldens Putin to expand his aggression. “Why are two real estate agents pushing this idea?” Ilves said referring to Kushner and Steve Witkoff, another Trump envoy, both of whom made their fortunes in real estate before entering diplomacy. “These people aren’t even diplomats,” said Ilves, who led his former Soviet republic from 2006 to 2016. “I’m not sure they have much of an idea of the long history of the development of security architecture in Europe relating to Russia.” Asked about the criticisms, assistant White House press secretary Olivia Wales said the U.S. proposal sought to “strengthen existing European security arrangements, with NATO at their core, while developing practical mechanisms to prevent future conflict.” Security guarantees for Ukraine “cannot be designed without understanding the broader security framework in which they will operate,” she said in an email, adding that any final agreement must respect Europe and Ukraine’s sovereignty “and be agreed by the relevant parties.” European officials are nonetheless unnerved by Kushner’s remarks. Kallas, the E.U. foreign policy chief, described Russia’s maximalist war demands as “really absurd,” while German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul pointed out that “Europe has a security architecture — we don’t need a new one.” Elsewhere, Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said the rules were not the issue: “The problem is that Russia is breaking them.” And even Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney was adamant that the “security architecture for free Europe will be determined by free Europe and NATO, not by Russia.” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the idea as “dangerous,” saying that European security “should not be the main agenda.” Ukraine’s view is that Russia is in no place to make such demands, given that it’s spent more than four years failing to win the war. “At this stage, the most Putin can negotiate is a fair ceasefire along the current line of contact,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said. And “frankly, Europe does not need a new security order; it already exists, and Russia is constantly violating it.” Kyiv and its European backers also argue that a ceasefire must come before any peace talks, accusing Russia of stalling so it can keep bombing civilian infrastructure ahead of the frigid winter. If Europe accepts Russia’s demands about wider continental security before there is a ceasefire, Moscow “will try to create the impression that it’s our fault that the war continues, because we don’t want to accept all their demands,” according to Sven Biscop, a director at the Egmont Institute, a Belgian think tank. He said he believed dialogue with Russia is a good thing, a view echoed by influential Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who in an interview with the Financial Times published Tuesday said that it had been “irresponsible” to outsource talks with Putin to the U.S., which he said could be leaning toward carving up Europe into spheres of influence. Back in Washington, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., urged Trump’s team to refuse Putin’s demands. The Russian leader not only wanted control of Ukraine but “he wants to redesign NATO to accommodate his revisionist ambitions,” Shaheen said, adding that any discussions about European security infrastructure should be a “nonstarter,” for the U.S. which “has benefited from the Alliance.” Amid all of this, any substantial progress toward ending the war remains elusive. The latest round of talks between the U.S., Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, last week produced no major breakthrough. Kushner said Washington was working toward what could be the largest prisoner swap of the war, while reporting that Russia had agreed to give Europe a seat at the table during the next round. Russia hasn’t quite confirmed that, instead saying that it needs “to understand from the Europeans themselves” what they can “contribute to the peace process” before allowing them to join, as Putin’s spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters Monday. There has been some internal wrangling among the European nations about who might represent them. Leaders have agreed on a team comprising the United Kingdom (which left the E.U. in 2020), France, Germany, Italy and Poland, alongside representatives of the European Commission and European Council. Kallas herself was left off the team. “I don’t know who among the current leaders could be a sane dialogue partner,” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the state-run news agency Tass on Monday. He likened the chosen group of European countries to “the Quartet,” a satirical poem by Russian author Ivan Krylov. In it, a monkey, a donkey, a goat and a bear blame their failure to form a string quartet on the seating arrangement rather than their lack of musical ability. That, at least, involved agreeing to a seating arrangement.

articles.title: 'It was really scary': Mother describes sheltering during Russia strikes on Kyiv bridge
articles.summary: Moscow has targeted bridges in Kyiv, while Ukraine severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea.
articles.body:
The alarms warning of a ballistic missile threat went off just before 23:30 on Monday in Kyiv. Moments later came the boom of explosions.

Once again, the main bridges over the broad River Dnipro that cuts through the city were the target and this time the Russian missiles hit what they wanted.

Close to one end of the Pivnichnyi (Northern) bridge there is a large crater and in the pouring rain, water now rushes through it to the river below. Chunks of tarmac and metal are scattered around.

At its broadest point, the jagged hole is about eight metres wide.

The crossing is closed to all traffic apart from the occasional fire engine or police car passing at high speed. By contrast, nearby roads are jammed with cars and trucks, forced to take long detours.

Anyone in a hurry to move around this city has to walk, or cycle, across the bridge, picking their way through the wreckage. In the miserable weather, that also means getting very wet.

Masha and her family moved to a flat next to the bridge because they had been living by a power plant that kept getting hit by Russian missiles.

Last night, she was in the kitchen of their new place when the Russians struck the bridge. She thought her windows would be blown out of their frames by the explosions.

"It was really scary. We had no idea they'd hit here so much. It's like we're cursed," Masha told me, describing grabbing her child and running into the corridor for protection.

But somehow, she still managed to sound cheerful.

"It's difficult, but we're used to it. And we try to take the positive from everything. Like: we survived today! So we can be happy about that."

From the damage, it looks like Russia targeted the same spot on the bridge with a volley of three missiles, aiming to keep the road closed for as long as possible.

A major recovery operation is under way, with firefighters and engineers in fluorescent overalls working to evaluate the extent of the damage. But it looks like the disruption will continue for some time.

Further along the Dnipro River, the Pivdennyi (Southern) bridge was also hit on Monday night, with four missiles.

The metro line across it was suspended for a while, although by mid-afternoon it had been restored. The mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said road transport in one direction was also being partially restored.

On the Pivnichnyi bridge, a man with a bag of tennis rackets on his back was gazing at the crater in front of him. He was heading home from the courts after he had travelled on foot to the left bank.

"It is upsetting," Anatolii told us. "Then when you read the news of what our side did to the Crimea bridge, you do feel a bit better."

That is because there was a battle of the bridges overnight.

Ukrainian missiles hit the one Russia had built to occupied Crimea, and caused serious damage. That bridge is prized by Russian President Vladimir Putin personally, a symbol of his illegal 2014 takeover.

Ukrainians loathe it for the same reason and now a section has collapsed into the sea, along with its towering arch.

To many here, the timing feels significant: a blow to Putin's image, just as he wants to seem most powerful at this week's summit with the US and China.

But for Kyiv resident Antonina, today is just another challenge to overcome.

The 67-year-old, who we met pulling a shopping trolley through the debris on a bridge in the Ukrainian capital, was heading to see her son on the right bank, but taxi drivers were charging a fortune to go round, so she decided to walk.

"It was a very scary night. It felt like something exploded right over my head. We will get through this, but I just wish the war would end."

articles.title: Huntingdon train attacker feared 'conspiracy by devil', jury told
articles.summary: Anthony Williams denies trying to murder 10 people on a train which stopped in Cambridgeshire.
articles.body:
A knifeman accused of trying to kill passengers on a moving train had a delusional belief his life was at risk because of a "conspiracy by the devil", a court has heard.

Anthony Williams denies 10 counts of attempted murder on a Doncaster to London King's Cross service which had to make an unscheduled stop at Huntingdon in Cambridgeshire on 1 November last year.

Cambridge Crown Court heard Dr Bernard Chin, a consultant forensic psychiatrist instructed by the defence, diagnosed Williams with schizophrenia.

Williams, 33, of Langford Road, Peterborough, denies four other counts of attempted murder in relation to earlier attacks in his home city and London.

At the start of the defence case, barrister Gillian Jones KC told jurors: "I'm not going to call Mr Williams to give evidence."

The judge, Mr Justice Calver, told jurors: "You must not hold this against him in any way."

Chin was taken through the background by Jones, and the court heard how, on 30 September, Williams had contacted his GP "highlighting his deteriorating mental state" and that his medication was not working.

Jurors were told the GP had found the defendant had only been taking 100mg of his medication, when he should have been taking 200mg.

A meeting had been arranged but "he didn't respond or attend that meeting", the court was told.

Williams contacted his GP again on 23 October but jurors heard he "didn't respond to the GP calling back".

Chin said a report had been written by psychiatrist Dr Alan Smith when Williams was in custody the day after the train attack. It had noted Williams thought there had been a "conspiracy organised by the devil against him and everyone was part of the conspiracy against him".

Jones, summarising the report by Smith, said Williams "had stopped his quetiapine, the medication, three days prior as it wasn't working though he acknowledged the voices got worse after".

He added Williams said he had believed there was a "conspiracy" accusing him of being "a paedophile".

He is accused of attempting to murder three people in Peterborough - two of them on a footbridge over the River Nene - on 31 October, the day before the attack on the LNER service.

"I was extremely paranoid then... I was going to be run over by cars," the court heard Williams had told Chin, adding he "went to the river because no cars could run me over there".

The same night he had gone into a barber shop brandishing a knife and he was reported to state how "voices were telling me they were going to attack me".

On the LNER service, he was reported to have said he had heard announcements on the train's speakers saying "these people are going to attack you".

Jurors heard Williams had said to Chin: "I just needed to protect myself. It was me or them."

The court has been told that after his arrest, he punched a police officer while in custody.

Williams, the court heard, had been hearing voices telling him the officer had been calling him a paedophile.

Chin said he had diagnosed Williams with schizophrenia, an opinion shared with an expert for the prosecution, and that "he experiences his thoughts being broadcast out".

Whether Williams carried out the attacks is not in question, the court has been told, but jurors must consider whether he intended to kill.

Chin said he was satisfied Williams had been "suffering from an acute relapse of schizophrenia at the time of each of the alleged offences".

He "retained the capacity to form intent" and the defence of insanity had not been met.

He said Williams "had what we call paranoid persecutory delusions, meaning he had ideas and beliefs that people were going to harm him and that this was an organised conspiracy that came about due to… the devil".

The jurors were told Williams had the "the delusional premise that his life was at risk by a wide-ranging conspiracy by the devil".

Chin said it was likely Williams had been intoxicated but this was "unlikely to have caused or sustained the psychosis".

As well as arguing Williams had been attempting to murder 10 people on the train, prosecutors allege that on 31 October he tried to kill three people in Peterborough.

He is also charged with attempting to murder a teenager in the early hours of 1 November on a DLR train in east London.

articles.title: A woman believed Korean actor Lee Dong-wook wanted to marry her after 8 months of online chats; she reportedly lost 35 million won after his impersonator claimed an expensive overseas gift was stuck at customs
articles.summary: A woman in her 30s in South Korea reportedly lost 35 million won after spending eight months communicating online with someone pretending to be popular
articles.body: A woman in her 30s in South Korea reportedly lost 35 million won after spending eight months communicating online with someone pretending to be popular Korean actor Lee Dong-wook. The woman, who works as a background actor, believed the celebrity had developed romantic feelings for her and wanted to marry her. Their conversations eventually turned into discussions about meeting each other's families. However, the relationship was a carefully constructed romance scam, with the impersonator using a supposed overseas gift delivery to persuade her to transfer money.How the Lee Dong-wook impersonation turned into an 8-month romance scamAccording to SBS News, the woman, identified only as A, began communicating with someone claiming to be Lee Dong-wook through social media early in 2026. The conversations continued for approximately 8 months, during which she became convinced that she was speaking to the actual actor.The woman reportedly worked as a background actor and had been a fan of Lee Dong-wook for a long time. The impersonator gradually built a relationship with her through regular messages, compliments and affectionate conversations. They began to write to each other personally, and she thought that the actor had picked her out for a mistress.The Korea Times reported that the woman described the relationship as something that had developed naturally over several months. She believed the actor had expressed his feelings for her and considered her someone he wanted to marry.The woman believed they were preparing to meet each other's familiesAs the conversations continued, the impersonator reportedly made the relationship appear more serious by discussing their future together. According to SBS News, the woman said they exchanged selfies and complimented each other's appearances. The person also told her that she was beautiful and made her believe that his feelings were genuine.Their conversations eventually extended to the possibility of a formal meeting between their families, a step that made the woman believe marriage was becoming a realistic possibility.The Korea Times reported that the woman used affectionate Korean expressions during their conversations. She called the person oppa, a familiar term used by women for older men, while he addressed her with affectionate words.The woman thought the person was trying to keep the relationship going, as well. The impersonator also shared some advice about life in the entertainment industry, using her own experience as a background actor to build up a personal connection, The Herald Business reports.However, despite months of communication and discussions about marriage, the two had never met in person. They had also never spoken over the telephone. Their entire relationship existed through social media and private messaging.A supposed overseas gift became the reason for repeated money demandsThe financial requests reportedly began when the impersonator claimed to have sent the woman an expensive gift package while filming overseas. According to SBS News, he told her that the parcel contained presents worth approximately 700 million won but had been held up at customs.The person then claimed that money was needed to complete customs-clearance procedures and pay storage charges before the package could be delivered. The woman believed the explanation and started transferring money to the bank accounts provided by the impersonator.The Herald Business reported that the requests continued under the explanation that documentation and processing fees had to be paid to release the package. The woman made several transfers, even though the bank account holder names kept changing.The impersonator reportedly explained that his identity as a celebrity needed to remain private. This gave the woman a reason to accept the use of different bank accounts without questioning the arrangement.According to The Korea Times, the woman eventually transferred 35 million won, equivalent to approximately $23,700. The money was sent over the course of the online relationship, and she was unable to recover it.She broke into her savings to meet the impersonator's demandsThe financial impact became particularly serious when the woman began using money she had put aside for her own living expenses. SBS News reported that she broke her regular savings account and added money intended for daily expenses to meet the requests.The Herald Business also reported that she had used money from her fixed savings account to make the transfers. Despite the repeated payments, the promised gift never arrived, and she did not receive any of the money back.What is most troubling about the incident is that the woman reportedly continued to believe she was talking to Lee Dong-wook even after transferring large sums of money. The regular messages and affectionate conversations had convinced her that the relationship was genuine.Lee Dong-wook's agency warns fans about impersonation accountsFollowing the incident, Lee Dong-wook's management agency, Kingkong by Starship, issued a warning about people pretending to be its artists through private messaging services and social media accounts.According to The Herald Business, the agency clarified that its artists never ask individuals for money, valuables or personal information through private communication channels. It also warned that celebrities do not personally approach fans to request payments under the excuse of arranging exclusive or VIP fan meetings.The incident is not the first reported romance scam involving a well-known Korean actor. The Korea Times also referred to an earlier case involving an impersonator posing as actor Lee Jung-jae. A woman in her 50s reportedly lost approximately 500 million won after believing she was in a relationship with him.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Gavin Newsom sued by prosecutors and victim rights group to stop mass death row commutation
articles.summary: Prosecutors and loved ones of murder victims asked California’s high court on Monday to take action against Gov.
articles.body: Prosecutors and loved ones of murder victims asked California’s high court on Monday to take action against Gov. Gavin Newsom, claiming he overstepped his power in seeking to commute the death sentences of more than 500 condemned killers. Only the state’s Supreme Court can stop Newsom’s “disregard of the law — his abuse of power,” according to a lawsuit filed by the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation (CJLF). The victim rights group filed its action on behalf of 30 county district attorneys and more than two dozen family members of those slain by killers now sitting on California’s death row. Newsom failed to give proper notice to “the victims of these heinous crimes,” thus denying grieving loved ones the “opportunity to be heard before a commutation decision,” according to the plaintiffs. The mass commutations were also made without mandated “individualized consideration of the intended recipients,” plaintiffs said. “Thousands of jurors and hundreds of judges set aside their personal views on the merits of the death penalty to render judgments based on the evidence and the law,” according to the filing by CJLF president and CEO Anne Marie Schubert, the former district attorney of Sacramento County. “Governor Newsom decided his personal views should override all those who actually participated in the process, followed and applied the law,” Schubert added. A representative for Newsom did not immediately respond to an NBC News request for comment on Tuesday. Earlier this month, Newsom announced that he intends to commute all California death sentences, declaring that “state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with” values in America’s most populous state. The governor, in an open letter to constituents, said that this move was “among the most difficult of my career.” Newsom moved to grant clemency to 548 people, 529 men and 19 women, who are currently sentenced to death in California. The state constitution mandates that California’s high court must approve gubernatorial clemency to anyone convicted of more that one felony, meaning it’d have to sign off on 382 of those proposed commutations, according to Newsom. Whether Newsom can issue a blanket order on the fate of those condemned inmates is uncharted territory. “This is all new and we don’t really have answers,” said Michael Vitiello, a professor at the University of the Pacific’s McGeorge School of Law. “There’s no record (of a previous mass commutation). This is not something that we have a great deal of precedent.” But if there’s no detailed mandate for judicial review, University of California Law San Francisco professor Hadar Aviram said the governor’s action isn’t subject to extensive scrutiny from the bench. “This is an executive decision, it’s not a judicial decision,” Aviram said Tuesday. “It doesn’t require any sort of legal proceedings with respect to each person individually. There is nothing to stop the governor from using this authority.” A 2018 procedural order from the high court might’ve signaled its desire to avoid expressing “a substantive view on the merits of an application.” “The California Supreme Court has recognized that the power to choose mercy is uniquely in the hands of the governor and the court’s role in this process is extremely limited,” said University of California Berkeley law professor Ty Alper, co-director of the school’s Death Penalty Clinic. The Golden State hasn’t put a prisoner to death since Jan. 17, 2006, when Clarence Ray Allen was executed via lethal injection. While the plaintiffs appear to have the general backing of California law enforcement, at least a handful of district attorneys support Newsom’s action. “As a prosecutor, I believe that we will remain safer from crime and injustice as long as we believe that we can and should change outdated and ineffective practices like the death penalty,” five-term Santa Clara County DA Jeff Rosen said in a statement released by Smart Justice California, a criminal justice reform advocacy group. Rosen added: “We must always work toward a better criminal justice system. We will be a safer community if we never lose faith in human dignity, including our own.”

articles.summary: LONDON: Sex offender Jeffrey Epstein did not die by suicide and was strangled in his jail cell, according to a consultant in forensic medicine who is the
articles.body: LONDON: Sex offender Jeffrey Epstein did not die by suicide and was strangled in his jail cell, according to a consultant in forensic medicine who is the first to have access to the medical examiner’s full records.Dr Michael Freeman, fellow of the Royal College of Pathologists in London, who has doctorates in epidemiology and forensic medicine, was given exclusive access to the examiners’ report by Epstein’s brother Mark, and has spent the past year examining it.He gave a lecture at Middle Temple, an inn of court, in London on Monday night in which he claimed that the most likely cause of death was “assault and a struggle” followed by “homicide strangulation from behind”, pointing out the mark on Epstein’s neck did not look like a hanging mark and fingernail marks above the ligature mark on Epstein’s neck, were consistent with strangulation.He said that a deep haemorrhage in Epstein’s left shoulder and cuts on his mouth were consistent with “blunt force trauma”, suggesting assault and struggle, adding: “The pattern, distribution and multitude of injuries are not consistent with a suicidal hanging. Homicide is the only remaining explanation.”“The evidence is most consistent with an assault, a ligature strangulation from behind and then most probably using that same ligature to suspend the body from the bunkbed,” Freeman told BBC Newsnight. “He did not get all of those injuries from self-inflicted hanging. He didn’t die from a natural cause, old age or an accident, and so the only option we have is homicide.”Mark Epstein, who attended the event, told the Times in the UK: “We now know that he was killed: so who killed him and, second, who had him killed? Who would be in a position to orchestrate this in a federal prison, and be in a position to cover it up? It’s a very small list.”Freeman, whose research has not been peer reviewed, has released all the files to pCloud.The New York City Office of Chief Medical Examiner, which conducted Epstein’s autopsy, said it “stands by its determination” of suicide.On Aug 10, 2019 two prison officers at the Metropolitan Correctional Centre in New York had found Epstein, awaiting trial on sex-trafficking charges, hanged from his bunkbed.You use AI every day. articles.title: Pizza Hut returns to its beloved roots nearly 70 years after $600 start
articles.summary: From a $600 loan to a $300 million PepsiCo sale, Dan Carney helped build Pizza Hut into the world's largest pizza chain, now embracing its nostalgic past.
articles.body: The death of Pizza Hut co-founder Dan Carney at the age of 95 marks the end of an era for one of America's most recognizable restaurant chains — a brand that is now turning to its past to attract a new generation of customers. What began as a small pizza restaurant in Wichita, Kansas, in 1958 grew into a global empire known for its distinctive red roofs, family dining rooms and nostalgic atmosphere. Carney and his younger brother, Frank, borrowed $600 from their mother, Mary, and purchased secondhand equipment to open their first Pizza Hut, according to the Kansas Historical Society. FIREHOUSE SUBS CO-FOUNDER DIES AFTER BUILDING BELOVED AMERICAN SANDWICH CHAIN WITH BROTHER The restaurant quickly caught on, and the brothers opened their first franchised location in Topeka, Kansas, the following year. By 1971, Pizza Hut had become the world's largest pizza restaurant chain in both sales and number of locations, according to the company's website. Six years later, the brothers sold Pizza Hut to PepsiCo for approximately $300 million. As the chain expanded, it developed a recognizable identity, including Pizza Pete, a mustachioed cartoon mascot sporting a checkered neckerchief, apron and hat. AMERICA'S BEST-TASTING PIZZA CHAIN IS AN OLD-SCHOOL FAVORITE, SURVEY FINDS The character was created by Ed Pointer, an illustrator and fraternity brother of Dan Carney, according to Wichita State University's Pizza Hut Museum. Pete appeared on advertisements, drinking cups, bags and restaurant signs, becoming one of the company's earliest recognizable symbols. Pizza Hut also became a fixture of American family dining, with its signature red-roof restaurants, vinyl booths, stained-glass-style lamps and red plastic drinking cups. RESTAURANTS BRING BACK OLD-SCHOOL HOSPITALITY AS NOSTALGIA TAKES HOLD ACROSS AMERICA For generations of Americans, a trip to Pizza Hut meant more than grabbing a slice. It was a destination for birthday parties, family dinners and celebrations. But as dining habits changed, the chain increasingly shifted toward delivery and carryout, leaving many of its traditional sit-down restaurants behind. Nearly seven decades after its founding, some Pizza Hut franchisees are betting that the chain's past could help shape its future. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The Pizza Hut Classic concept, which began around 2017, brings back the familiar atmosphere of the 1980s and 1990s, complete with checkerboard tablecloths, Tiffany-style lamps and other vintage touches. The throwback restaurants have become a hit with customers, some traveling hours to relive childhood memories. Tim Sparks, president of Wichita, Kansas-based Daland Corp., which operates dozens of dine-in Pizza Hut restaurants, previously told Fox News Digital that the nostalgic atmosphere has struck a chord with diners. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS In Homosassa Springs, Florida, dine-in sales more than doubled after a restaurant was converted to the classic format, FOX 13 Tampa Bay reported. Sparks said the restaurants also appear to encourage something increasingly rare in modern dining: customers putting down their phones and enjoying conversations. Today, the original 1958 Pizza Hut building stands on the campus of Wichita State University, where it serves as a museum celebrating the chain's history. Visitors can even pose for photographs with a likeness of Pizza Pete, whose image remains a permanent fixture at the museum. articles.title: A diver identified an East India Company ship that sank off the Isles of Scilly in 1680 after years of research and underwater exploration; its recovered artefacts, including coins and sword fragments, are now going on display
articles.summary: A collection of artefacts recovered from a 17th-century shipwreck has been donated to the Isles of Scilly Museum.
articles.body: A collection of artefacts recovered from a 17th-century shipwreck has been donated to the Isles of Scilly Museum. The finds came from the Phoenix, an East India Company vessel that sank off the islands in 1680 while returning from China with cargo. Local diver and author Todd Stevens donated the collection after identifying the wreck in 2017.His search followed years of investigation and exploration. According to the Isles of Scilly Museum, material includes coins, navigational instruments, sword fragments, jewellery and items believed to have belonged to the crew and Captain William Wildy. The artefacts will be displayed in the museum’s Maritime Gallery, where visitors can explore the ship’s final voyage and the maritime history of the Isles of Scilly.How did Todd Stevens identify the shipwreck after years of searchingThe Phoenix was a 46-gun ship built at Blackwall in 1670. It was captained by William Wildy of Whitechapel and sailed under charter to the East India Company. The vessel was returning from Amoy, China, when it was wrecked in poor weather near the Isles of Scilly on 11 January 1680.Its cargo included pepper, spices, silks and cloth. The loss became part of the islands’ maritime history and had consequences beyond the ship and its cargo. Contemporary correspondence after the disaster showed that the wreck prompted the construction of a lighthouse on St Agnes. It was the first lighthouse built on the Isles of Scilly.How an old map and broken cannons helped identify the Phoenix wreckStevens traced the wreck site through years of historical investigation and underwater exploration. A historic map of the waters around the Isles of Scilly, held in the National Maritime Museum archive, helped him identify the area. The map had the words ‘Cap Wildy lost’ written across a section of sea west of the island of Samson.The note pointed towards the location associated with the Phoenix and its captain. After the site was located, documentary evidence helped establish the identity of the vessel. Distinctive ballast known as kentledge also confirmed the identification. The material consisted of broken cannon pieces carried aboard the ship. Stevens identified the wreck site in 2017, and later donated the recovered collection to the Isles of Scilly Museum.Recovered artefacts offer a glimpse into 17th-century life at seaThe donated collection contains many objects recovered from the Phoenix wreck. These include coins, navigational instruments, sword fragments, jewellery and other personal items. The museum said some of the personal belongings are believed to have belonged to members of the crew and Captain Wildy himself. The finds provide an insight into maritime trade, navigation and life at sea during the 17th century, in the 1600s.The collection was donated by Stevens, a local diver and author who identified the wreck site. Curator of the Isles of Scilly Museum, Dr Xavier Duffy, said, “The quality of the finds is outstanding – it’s hard to believe these items have been sitting on the seabed for nearly 350 years. This donation ensures the material can now be shared with the public and preserved for future generations as part of the islands’ heritage.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
