articles.title: More than 100,000 take part in France pay protests
articles.summary: Government says 146,000 take part in rallies across France, as CGT trade union put the nationwide total over 500,000.
articles.body:
More than 100,000 people have taken to the streets in France to protest against the high cost of living, with public sector workers demanding pay increases.

The Interior Ministry said on Tuesday that a total of 146,000 people took part in the protests, with 28,000 in Paris alone. The CGT trade union put the nationwide total at just over 500,000 demonstrators.

Several trade unions had called for a day of strike action. Participants included public sector workers, as well as school pupils and university students.

France’s 5.8 million public sector employees were pushed to mobilise after talks with Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on Friday failed to satisfy union demands. Union representatives left the meeting organised by Lecornu saying the proposed measures failed to address the urgency of the pay situation.

Tuesday’s rally is the third call for a united day of action and strikes in the public sector since September.

Unions have been pushing for across-the-board pay rises since last week’s boost to the minimum wage for private-sector workers.

Protesters say “they simply can’t make ends meet, and they want the government to help them put more money into funding in terms of salaries, in terms of raising the minimum wage”, Al Jazeera’s Natacha Butler reported from Paris.

“The government’s already offered about $30 extra a month on the minimum wage, but those here say that is simply not enough. With inflation, with the way the prices are going up, they say they actually need more.”

The unions put the loss of purchasing power for public servants at 16 percent since 2017, leading to increasing numbers of public employees ending up on or close to the minimum wage against a backdrop of inflation.

“The government doesn’t have much margin or wiggle room financially , because of France’s ballooning debt, and the government’s in the middle of trying to push through a budget with cost-cutting measures in it,” Butler said.

Public-sector workers aim to pressure the government to unfreeze the pay scale point used to calculate their basic salary. However, the government has ruled out any general pay rise for the fourth consecutive year in its draft budget.

“The people in the street know there is only so far you can go; the government knows they do not have a lot of economic wiggle room. Yet nobody really is coming up with another solution,” Butler said.

Despite the government’s efforts to ease tensions, demonstrations have roiled the country for over a month.

Student-led protests demanding better conditions in education erupted in mid-September, but the movement has since expanded in scope to cover a range of issues, from high fuel prices to wages and social housing

Protests for higher wages, lower costs of living and better public services have also spread across Europe.

articles.title: JetBlue flight from Puerto Rico to Florida hit by severe turbulence: 5 injured, what happened aboard Flight 1717?
articles.summary: Five people were injured after a JetBlue flight from Puerto Rico to Florida encountered severe turbulence shortly before landing at Fort
articles.body: Five people were injured after a JetBlue flight from Puerto Rico to Florida encountered severe turbulence shortly before landing at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport on Tuesday morning. JetBlue Flight 1717 was travelling from Ponce, Puerto Rico, to Fort Lauderdale when it encountered turbulence, prompting an emergency response at the airport.The Broward County Sheriff's Office Fire Rescue unit said it received reports of injuries aboard the aircraft at around 6:25 am local time. The plane landed safely at approximately 6:58 am and proceeded to Terminal 3, where emergency personnel were waiting to assess passengers and crew members who had reported injuries.“Fire rescue personnel identified five individuals reporting injuries or requiring evaluation,” the fire rescue unit said in a statement to CNN. The five individuals declined transportation to nearby hospitals, authorities said. There were no reports of structural damage to the aircraft.JetBlue confirmed that the flight had encountered turbulence and that medical personnel evaluated passengers and crew members after landing. “The safety of our customers and crewmembers remains our top priority,” the airline said in a statement.What caused the turbulence?The exact cause of the turbulence has not been established. However, CNN meteorologist Brandon Miller said thunderstorms were present over the Turks and Caicos and the southern Bahamas on Tuesday morning, areas the aircraft would likely have been navigating. Other aircraft operating in the region reported light to moderate turbulence, Miller said.The storms extended to altitudes of up to 46,000 feet, meaning aircraft in the area would have been attempting to avoid the strongest storm activity.There were no other reports of turbulence-related injuries on flights landing at Fort Lauderdale airport on Tuesday morning, according to Broward Sheriff Fire Rescue.Why can turbulence injure passengers even when a plane lands safely?Turbulence occurs when an aircraft encounters irregular air movements that can cause sudden changes in altitude, direction or speed.Although commercial aircraft are designed to withstand turbulence, passengers and crew members can be thrown against seats, overhead compartments or other parts of the cabin during sudden movements.The Federal Aviation Administration warns that turbulence can occur unexpectedly, including in clear skies, making it difficult for pilots and passengers to anticipate every encounter. Passengers are advised to keep their seat belts fastened whenever seated, even when the seat belt sign is switched off, to reduce the risk of injuries during unexpected turbulence.You use AI every day. articles.title: Church of England should protect 'every belief', King says
articles.summary: King Charles III was speaking at the opening of General Synod, the Church of England's national assembly
articles.body:
King Charles has said the Church of England does not just protect the Christian faith, but also the space "for every belief" within British society.

He was speaking in his role as Supreme Governor of the Church at the inauguration of a new term of its national assembly, General Synod.

While such comments have caused fierce theological debate in the past, they are consistent with the King's long-expressed beliefs.

Similar statements about the Church were also made by Queen Elizabeth II in a landmark speech given during her Diamond Jubilee.

The late Queen attended 10 Synod inauguration ceremonies since the assembly was established in 1970, though the then Earl of Wessex attended on her behalf at the last inauguration in 2021.

The day's ceremony started with a worship service at Westminster Abbey. The King and members of Synod then moved the short distance to Church House, the Church's administrative headquarters, for the Sovereign's address.

Speaking to the nearly 500 members of the assembly - including all the Church's bishops as well as clergy and lay people, many of whom were newly elected for a 5-year term - the King talked of his own deep faith and the way it guided him.

He then talked of a clear vision of the Church's public role.

"At a time when our society can feel divided, it is all the more important that the Church of England continues to extend its ministry among all the people of this country," the King said.

"The Church protects not just the Christian faith of all of us gathered in this room, but the very space for faith itself – of every belief – within our whole society and national discourse," he continued.

In an interview in 1994, the then Prince of Wales caused controversy by talking of a desire to be seen as "Defender of Faith" rather than "Defender of the Faith", the term by which sovereign leaders of the Church of England are referred.

He later clarified that his comments had been misinterpreted, saying he never intended to abandon his Church of England role, but could also act as a "protector of faiths" having long talked and written passionately about interfaith harmony and protecting everyone's right to worship.

In 2023 the King maintained his traditional coronation oaths, including a vow to be "Defender of the Faith", while also prominently incorporating multi-faith elements into the coronation ceremony.

But the King's comments today are reminiscent of a speech given by Queen Elizabeth II to an interfaith audience at Lambeth Palace in 2012.

She spoke of the role of the Church of England often being misunderstood, saying its duty was not to exclusively defend Anglicanism, or to exclude other religions, but to protect the free practice of all faiths in the UK.

Speaking today, the King did not speak directly of other contentious issues facing the Church such as safeguarding, or Christian nationalism, slavery reparations or the financial pressures on parishes

But it is clear that while this was something of a celebratory day for the Church, and particularly for the new members of Synod, there will be solemn and serious work to be done in the coming years.

articles.title: States put speed-limiting devices in reckless drivers' cars
articles.summary: Virginia's GPS speed limiter program is already active for reckless driving offenders, but early users report glitches that apply wrong speed limits.
articles.body: We've all seen it. You're driving down the highway when someone flies past you at a ridiculous speed. Maybe they're weaving through traffic while everyone else tries to stay out of their way. Now, states are turning to speed-limiting devices that could stop some of the most dangerous drivers from doing it again. Virginia has already started installing GPS-powered devices in vehicles used by certain reckless-driving offenders. Washington, D.C., has a similar program, and more jurisdictions are exploring the technology. The idea sounds promising. Instead of simply telling someone to slow down, the device can actually restrict how fast their car accelerates. However, there's a catch. Some drivers using these systems have reported GPS glitches that mistakenly apply the speed limits of nearby roads. And that raises a question worth asking. What happens when your car refuses to accelerate because its GPS thinks you're somewhere else? Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. SILICON VALLEY DEVELOPER ACCUSED OF MURDER AFTER INVESTIGATORS SAY TESLA REACHED 142 MPH BEFORE FATAL CRASH How speed-limiting devices stop reckless drivers The technology is called Intelligent Speed Assistance (ISA). It uses GPS location information and digital maps to determine the posted speed limit. Here's how it works. Let's say you're traveling on a road with a 45 mph speed limit. As your vehicle reaches 45 mph, the device restricts additional acceleration. Pressing harder on the gas pedal won't normally make the car accelerate beyond that limit. However, the system doesn't automatically slam on the brakes or shut off the engine. Instead, it limits the vehicle's ability to accelerate. That means a vehicle traveling downhill could still exceed the posted limit because of gravity. Some systems also allow brief overrides when additional acceleration is necessary for safety. Think of it as a speed governor that automatically adjusts as you move between roads. The important difference comes down to control. Many newer vehicles already recognize speed limits and warn drivers when they're going too fast. These aftermarket devices take things further by restricting acceleration. Virginia is already putting speed limiters in cars Virginia launched its Intelligent Speed Assistance Program on July 1. The state allows courts to require speed-limiting technology for certain driving offenses, including reckless driving and racing. The Virginia DMV can also require participation in qualifying cases involving excessive demerit points. For eligible drivers, the program offers a way to maintain restricted driving privileges rather than face a full license suspension. According to a Nov. 2 report, approximately 100 devices had been installed in Virginia since July. Many participants faced reckless-driving charges or convictions. Some cases involved speeds exceeding 100 mph. The restrictions are serious. Qualifying drivers may need the equipment installed in every vehicle they own or co-own. They must also comply with restrictions on which vehicles they can operate. Then there's the cost. Participants generally pay installation and ongoing service fees, although financial assistance may be available for those who qualify. The goal is to let certain drivers continue essential travel while reducing the risk of dangerous speeding. More states are moving toward speed-limiting technology Virginia has company in exploring this approach. Washington, D.C. launched its Intelligent Speed Assistance Program on Oct. 1, 2025. Under the program, D.C. driver's license holders convicted of aggravated reckless driving must enroll and operate only authorized vehicles equipped with the technology. Washington state passed legislation in 2025 requiring speed-limiting devices in certain cases involving dangerous speeding and driving restrictions. However, those requirements won't take effect until Jan. 1, 2029. Meanwhile, New York City is considering a proposal introduced on Oct. 22. It would require vehicle owners who accumulate 16 school-zone speeding violations within 12 months to install speed-limiting devices. The New York City proposal remains in committee and has not become law. These programs differ in scope. Still, they show how policymakers are increasingly considering technology as a response to dangerous driving. JOE BIDEN MANDATED ALL NEW VEHICLES COME INSTALLED WITH A 'KILL SWITCH.' THIS REPUBLICAN WANTS TO REPEAL IT GPS glitches are raising serious safety concerns GPS technology is incredibly useful. But anyone who's followed navigation directions onto the wrong road knows it can make mistakes. Consider this situation. You're driving on a highway with a 65 mph speed limit. A service road running alongside it has a 35 mph limit. If your GPS mistakenly places you on the service road, the speed limiter could apply the lower limit. Your vehicle wouldn't suddenly brake, but it could restrict additional acceleration even though you're traveling on a highway with a higher speed limit. That's the type of GPS problem some Virginia participants have reported. Early users reportedly experienced situations where their devices applied lower limits from nearby roads. Officials acknowledged the complaints and said they were working on fixes. To be clear, the reports establish that location errors have occurred. They do not establish a pattern of crashes caused by those errors. That could become a safety concern when a driver needs additional acceleration to merge into traffic, but the vehicle won't respond as expected. That's a potential safety concern officials need to address before these systems become more widespread. Can drivers override a speed limiter in an emergency? Some systems provide temporary overrides when drivers need additional acceleration. Virginia's proposed technical standards outline specific limits for emergency overrides, although those requirements have not yet been finalized. Under the proposal, an override would last no longer than 30 seconds, permit a maximum of 5 mph above the posted speed limit and allow no more than two overrides per driving cycle. Those specifications appear in regulations published Oct. 19. The rules remain proposed, with public comments accepted through Dec. 18. The limits are intended to balance safety with the program's goal of preventing excessive speeding. However, they also show that an emergency override may provide much less acceleration than a driver expects. That's why clear instructions and reliable operation are so important. Why officials believe speed limiters could save lives There's a serious reason states are considering these devices. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, 11,288 people died in speeding-related traffic crashes in 2024. Speeding contributed to 29% of all U.S. traffic fatalities that year. Those numbers help explain why officials want something more effective than another speeding ticket. A driver who repeatedly ignores speed limits may continue taking risks after paying fines. And suspending someone's license doesn't physically prevent that person from getting behind the wheel. Speed-limiting technology offers another option. A properly functioning device can prevent certain excessive speeds while allowing qualifying drivers to continue traveling to work or handling essential responsibilities. However, speed limits tell only part of the safety story. Someone can drive recklessly without exceeding the posted limit. Following too closely can still cause a crash. Bad weather can also make a legally permitted speed dangerous. So, these devices may help reduce extreme speeding, but they cannot guarantee safe driving. NEW BIG RIG SAFETY TECH COULD SAVE YOUR LIFE Could speed limiters eventually be required in every car? That's the bigger question. For now, these enforcement programs focus on drivers who meet specific legal criteria. There is no nationwide requirement forcing every U.S. driver to install one of these aftermarket speed-limiting devices. However, many newer vehicles already offer speed-limit recognition and warnings. That means some of the technology has become familiar to drivers. The bigger step involves allowing software to actively restrict acceleration. As more jurisdictions test these programs, lawmakers could consider expanding eligibility. But any expansion would require additional policy decisions. And public acceptance could become a major obstacle. After all, there's a big difference between your dashboard warning you that you're speeding and your car preventing you from accelerating. Speed-limiting devices also raise privacy questions There's another issue I think deserves more attention. What happens to all the driving information these systems collect? GPS-based speed limiters need location data to determine which speed limit applies. Depending on the program, they may also record speeding events and other information used to monitor compliance. Virginia's proposed regulations would require service providers to report certain vehicle events and speed violations, including GPS locations. The proposal also contains a significant additional requirement. Beginning July 1, 2027, new installations would need cameras capable of photographing the driver's seat when the device records a speeding event, if the proposed rules take effect as written. That raises questions about who can access the information and how long it remains stored. We explored similar privacy concerns in our article, Is it worth saving money to let a car insurance company track your every move? Insurance tracking programs serve a different purpose. However, both technologies show how much information connected vehicles can generate about the people driving them. And once that information exists, clear rules about its collection and use become especially important. Kurt's key takeaways I understand why states want to take this approach. We've all shared the road with someone driving so recklessly that you wonder how they still have a license. And if technology can prevent someone from driving 100 mph through traffic, I see the appeal. What concerns me is putting that much authority in the hands of a GPS system that can make mistakes. I've seen enough technology glitches over the years to know that even sophisticated systems sometimes get things wrong. That's inconvenient when your phone sends you to the wrong address. It's a much bigger concern when you're behind the wheel. I also think states need to be careful about how they expand these programs. Targeting repeat dangerous drivers makes sense. Requiring everyone to surrender control of their vehicle would raise a very different set of questions. Before we go further, I'd like to see stronger evidence that these devices reduce crashes without creating new safety problems. Because ultimately, the goal should be safer roads. And that means making sure the technology earns our trust before we depend on it. Would you feel safer knowing reckless drivers have speed limiters in their cars, or does the idea of a GPS system controlling your accelerator worry you even more? articles.title: A Texas man died without children and left his property, money and animals to two named beneficiaries in a handwritten will; when a cousin challenged it, a judge ordered DNA testing, but an appeals court blocked the test
articles.summary: A Texas man who died without a spouse or children left his property, money, personal belongings and animals to two people named in a handwritten will.
articles.body: A Texas man who died without a spouse or children left his property, money, personal belongings and animals to two people named in a handwritten will. But when his first cousin once removed challenged the document, a probate judge ordered DNA testing to confirm their family connection. A Texas appeals court has now stopped the test, ruling that the lower court did not have the legal power to order it while the will dispute remains unresolved. The Texas Fourteenth Court of Appeals issued its decision on 17 November 2026 in a case involving Peter K. Demel and the estate of John Demel. The judges found that the probate court had wrongly ordered Peter to provide DNA samples before deciding whether John's handwritten will was valid.The ruling means Peter cannot be forced to undergo genetic testing under the existing order. The appeals court also instructed the probate court to cancel its direction requiring him to take the test. According to the judgment published by Justia, the case is recorded as In re Peter K. Demel, case number 14-26-00320-CV, from Probate Court No. 5 of Harris County, Texas. Justice Katy Boatman wrote the opinion, with Justices Wise and Hart joining her. The dispute centres on a handwritten will that named Roxanne Bourdon and Chris Quijada as the only beneficiaries of John's estate. Peter Demel, John's first cousin once removed, challenged the attempt to have the document accepted by the probate court.A handwritten will leaves the entire estate to two beneficiariesJohn Demel died without a wife or children. He left behind a handwritten will, legally known as a holographic will, naming Bourdon and Quijada as the people who would inherit his belongings and property. The document stated: "I Johnny Demel being of sound mind leave my Estate including all real estate properties, monies, personal belongings, and my animals to Roxanne Bourdon and Chris Quijada."Neither Bourdon nor Quijada was a legal heir through blood or marriage. Instead, John had clearly stated in the document that he wanted both individuals to receive his property, money, personal belongings and animals after his death. After John died, Chris Quijada filed an application with Harris County Probate Court No. 5 to have the handwritten will accepted for probate. He also requested letters testamentary, which would give him the legal power to manage the estate as its executor. As another option, Quijada asked the court to formally identify John's legal heirs in case the will could not be accepted.Both Bourdon and Quijada agreed that Quijada should serve as the independent executor of the estate. Peter Demel later entered the case by opposing Quijada's application and challenging the handwritten will. According to the Texas Fourteenth Court of Appeals, his challenge led to several hearings and arguments over whether he could be forced to undergo genetic testing.Probate judge initially rejects DNA testingThe probate court first rejected Quijada's request to make Peter undergo DNA testing. In its written decision, the judge said the court did not have the power to order the test under the Texas Estates Code. Texas law allows courts to order genetic testing in certain cases where they need to identify a person's legal heirs. But the probate judge explained that these rules mainly apply to cases involving biological children or people claiming inheritance rights through them. The court also found that Peter's family relationship with John was not disputed. This was enough to give him the legal right to challenge the handwritten will. The judge therefore decided that DNA testing was not needed to prove Peter's right to take part in the case. Quijada later asked the judge to reconsider the decision. His request challenged only the part of the ruling that recognised Peter's legal right to contest the will. He argued that this issue should only be decided after a trial.After holding another hearing, the probate judge changed the earlier decision and approved Quijada's request for genetic testing. The court then issued a written order directing Peter to undergo testing at the National Screening Center. It instructed him to provide samples "as requested by National Screening Center" and stated that the testing had to follow Subchapter F, Chapter 160 of the Texas Family Code. Peter objected to the new order. He filed a request asking the probate court to reconsider its decision, submitted a motion to exclude evidence, requested another hearing and sought the removal of the trial judge from the case. The probate court refused to change its decision. Peter then took the matter to the appeals court.Appeals court says judge lacked legal authorityPeter approached the Texas Fourteenth Court of Appeals and filed a petition for a writ of mandamus. He argued that the probate judge had gone beyond the powers allowed by law when ordering him to undergo DNA testing. When considering a mandamus petition, an appeals court checks whether the lower court clearly abused its discretion and whether the person challenging the decision has another suitable way to obtain legal relief. Under Texas law, a judge abuses their discretion when they act unreasonably or fail to understand and apply the law correctly. Justice Boatman and the other judges focused on Section 204.051 of the Texas Estates Code. This section deals with court-ordered genetic testing in certain probate cases.The appeals court explained that Section 204.051 applies only to formal proceedings to identify legal heirs under Chapter 202 of the Estates Code. It does not give judges automatic permission to order DNA tests whenever someone challenges a will. The judges rejected Quijada's argument that an application to have a will accepted for probate should automatically be treated as an heirship case. Under Chapter 202, a formal heirship proceeding is allowed only in certain situations. These include cases where someone dies without a valid will and no estate administration has taken place in Texas, where a will or estate administration leaves out property in Texas, or where a trustee needs to identify the legal heirs of someone who has died.The judges found that none of these situations applied to John's estate because his handwritten will appeared to leave all his property to Bourdon and Quijada. The panel referred to the Texas Supreme Court's decision in Frost National Bank v. Fernandez. That ruling supports the principle that a separate heirship proceeding is not allowed when a person leaves a will that distributes their entire estate.Heirship cannot be decided before the will challengeQuijada also argued that his alternative request for a formal decision identifying John's heirs gave the probate judge a reason to order DNA testing. The Fourteenth Court of Appeals disagreed. The judges explained that the request to identify the heirs could not yet be decided because the probate court first had to determine whether John's handwritten will was valid. If the court accepts the will, John's estate will pass to Bourdon and Quijada according to his written instructions. Only if Peter succeeds in challenging the will and the court finds that John died without a valid will would it become necessary to identify his legal heirs.The appeals panel referred to earlier decisions in United Fire Lloyds v. Tippin and Guajardo v. Chavana. These rulings support the view that a court cannot decide who the heirs are until it has established that the person died without a valid will. The judges also considered whether genetic testing was needed to confirm Peter's legal right to challenge the document. Under the Texas Estates Code, a person with an interest in an estate can challenge a will. This can include an heir, beneficiary, spouse, creditor or another person with a property right or financial claim against the estate.The court pointed out that Quijada's own sworn application to probate John's will identified Peter as an heir with a one-eighth interest in the estate. Both sides also agreed that John had died without a spouse or children. This meant Peter could inherit part of the estate if the handwritten will was rejected. The appeals judges therefore found that Peter already had a direct financial interest in the case. His legal right to challenge the will did not depend on the results of a DNA test.Court warns of harm from forced genetic testingThe appeals court also considered whether Peter could wait until the probate case ended before challenging the DNA testing order through a normal appeal. The judges decided that this would not provide enough legal protection. Orders requiring genetic testing generally cannot be challenged through an immediate standard appeal. The panel explained that waiting until the end of the case could expose Peter to the very harm he was trying to prevent. Genetic test results could be disclosed and used during the legal proceedings before an appeals court had a chance to decide whether the testing order was lawful.The judges referred to an earlier legal decision involving the Office of the Attorney General of Texas when considering the risks linked to genetic testing and the disclosure of private information. The Fourteenth Court of Appeals had already issued a temporary stay, which paused the DNA testing while it considered Peter's petition. The panel conditionally granted his request for a writ of mandamus. It directed Probate Court No. 5 to cancel the order requiring Peter to undergo genetic testing. The judges also lifted the temporary stay and rejected Quijada's request for attorney fees as a penalty against Peter.The decision does not determine whether John's handwritten will is legally valid or whether Bourdon and Quijada will receive his estate. That question remains before the Harris County probate court. For now, the appeals court has ruled that Peter cannot be forced to provide DNA samples under the disputed order. articles.title: I’m an Apple loyalist, but Samsung’s latest tablet won me over after just 6 weeks of use — here’s how
articles.summary: I used the Samsung Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra for six weeks. Here’s what I loved about its 14.6-inch screen, S Pen and battery life, and what to know before you buy.
articles.body: I have always been an Apple girlie. Working in a creative industry means that my work-issued laptop has always been a Macbook. Because of that, I’m just more comfortable with iOs devices. So, when I was given the opportunity to test the new Samsung Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra, I was intrigued. I have never used an Android device before and, if I am being honest, was skeptical that any device could make me stray from team Apple. Nonetheless, I wanted to give this new tablet a fair opportunity to impress me. So, for more than a month I used the Tab S12 Ultra as my do-everything device: streaming shows in bed, sketching and taking handwritten notes with the included S Pen, browsing online and more. Below, find out exactly how it turned my head, plus whether I think its features are worth the high price. What is the Samsung Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra? The Samsung Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra is Samsung’s top-end Android tablet. It has a 14.6-inch AMOLED display for brightness, sharpness, and color accuracy. It also has four speakers for impressive sound and it comes with an S Pen that can be used for drawing, taking notes, and signing documents. On the software side, the tablet includes Samsung’s Galaxy AI tools. The most notable is Note Assist in the Samsung Notes app, which formats, spell-checks, translates, and summarizes written notes, including handwriting made with the S Pen. For recordings of things like lectures or meetings, Transcribe Assist converts the audio to text, which can then be summarized in Samsung Notes — that alleviates the need for additional transcription apps if you’re someone who conducts lots of interviews like I do. The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra runs on the MediaTek Dimensity 9500 processor with 12GB of RAM, which gives it plenty of power for multitasking, creative apps, and the on-device AI features. It has an 11,600mAh battery rated for up to 23 hours of video playback, so it can easily last a full day of work, classes, or streaming. The 256GB Wi-Fi model is priced at $1,400, making it one of the pricier tablets on the market. My experience with the Samsung Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra Samsung sent me a review unit of the base model (12GB of RAM, 256GB of storage), and I used it every day for 6 weeks. While I own an iPad Mini, I tucked that away for the entirety of the time I tested this tablet so that I would use the Samsung device for anything I’d normally use my other tablet for. Read what stood out below. What I liked about it The display is the star of the show The 14.6-inch OLED screen is the reason to buy this tablet, and it never stopped impressing me. Colors are rich and saturated, blacks are inky, and the 120Hz refresh rate makes scrolling feel smooth. Watching my favorite shows on it felt closer to a small TV than a tablet, especially with the quad speakers, which get loud and sound full in landscape mode. The screen also stayed easy to read when I worked near a sunny window and was big enough that I didn’t have to squint to see things even when I had a ton of pages open in my browser. It’s shockingly thin and lightweight At 5.1 millimeters, the Tab S12 Ultra is thinner than most phones, and at about 1.5 pounds it’s lighter than it looks. It slid into my tote next to my laptop with room to spare, and on several days I left my laptop behind entirely. The IP68 rating — which means it’s protected from spills and even dunks in water (though I wouldn’t suggest putting this to the test) — is a nice bonus I didn’t expect to appreciate. I stopped worrying about using it in the kitchen for following recipes. The S Pen is included, and it’s genuinely useful Unlike Apple, which sells its Pencil separately, Samsung includes the S Pen in the box. Writing feels natural, and it snaps magnetically to the back of the tablet when you’re not using it. Though, I purchased an inexpensive case for the tablet on Amazon and it has a slot for the pen at the top. I used the pen most in Samsung Notes, where Note Assist can tidy up and summarize handwritten copy. Adobe Photoshop also comes preinstalled for the first time on an Android tablet, which makes the Ultra a surprisingly capable canvas for creative work. It handles multitasking like a laptop The tablet runs on MediaTek’s Dimensity 9500 processor. That’s the chip that does all the work — think of it as the tablet’s “brain.” It kept everything fast and smooth in my testing, from juggling a dozen browser tabs to playing games. The tablet runs One UI 9, which is Samsung’s operating system. With it you can run up to three apps side by side, and the big screen gives each one enough room. I often had a video call, a document and Samsung Notes open at the same time. When I wanted something closer to a laptop, I switched on Samsung DeX. This mode makes the tablet look and work like a regular computer, with windows you can resize and a taskbar along the bottom for switching between apps. Battery life lasts through a full day (sometimes more) Samsung rates the 11,600mAh battery for up to 23 hours of video playback. Honestly, in my use, I rarely thought about the battery at all, which is the highest compliment I can give. I probably had to charge it every four to five days and that was with pretty constant use. Samsung also promises seven years of software and security updates, so this tablet should stay current well into the next decade. Potential drawbacks to note It’s expensive, and accessories add up The $1,399.99 starting price is not for anyone on a tight budget, and a keyboard cover and charger cost extra. That means that if you want the full laptop-replacement setup, you will have to budget a few hundred dollars more. The size isn’t for everyone A 14.6-inch tablet is wonderful on a desk or propped on your lap, but some may find it unwieldy to hold in one hand for long reading sessions. If you mostly want a tablet for reading in bed or on the subway, the slightly smaller Tab S12+ may suit you better. Some Android apps also don’t take full advantage of the giant screen, though Samsung’s apps and the major productivity apps I used looked great. Who is the Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra for? The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra is for anyone who wants the biggest, best screen they can get in a tablet, especially Android and Samsung phone owners. It’s a great fit for students who take handwritten notes, artists and designers who’ll put the S Pen and Photoshop to work, and frequent travelers who want one device for movies on the plane and email at the hotel. With a keyboard cover, it can replace a laptop for a lot of everyday work. Is the Samsung Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra worth it? I went into this review fully expecting to miss my Apple devices, and instead I was surprised by how much I loved the Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra. It feels big without being bulky or heavy, so I ended up taking it everywhere. The picture is better than any other device I own — truly, after six weeks I still found myself admiring the screen. I was also nervous about switching to Android for the first time, but it turned out to be easy to learn. I was finding my way around comfortably within a few days. It isn’t cheap, but if you want a big, beautiful screen in a tablet that can handle both work and play, the Tab S12 Ultra is worth it. It’s the first device that has ever made me question my loyalty to Apple. Why trust NBC Selected? I am a commerce editor at NBC Selected and a journalist who regularly covers tech and lifestyle, among other topics. I have recently written about red light therapy and sleep, wellness tech brand HigherDose and more. For this piece, I used the Samsung Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra daily for six weeks, doing things that the average person would do with their tablet, and took comprehensive notes about the experience. Catch up on NBC Selected’s in-depth coverage of tech and tools, wellness and more, and follow us on Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok to stay up to date.

articles.title: FEMA just tested its Emergency Alert System. Here's why.
articles.summary: FEMA tested the Emergency Alert System on TVs and radios nationwide Tuesday. Cell phones did not receive the alert.
articles.body:
TVs and radios nationwide broadcast an emergency alert on Tuesday. But don't be alarmed; it was only a test. We repeat: It was only a test.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), along with the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), ran the alert to ensure the Emergency Alert System (EAS) for radio and television will work during an actual emergency, such as a natural disaster, terrorist attack or other threat to public safety.

Wireless phones did not receive the test alert.

The test was conducted amid online conspiracy theories that there would be a 90-day power outage starting Tuesday, which only intensified after last week's Microsoft global Outlook outage and the Federal Aviation Administration's rare ground stop. The federal government has not announced a nationwide 90-day blackout or plans to shut down the U.S. power grid. The rumors are centered around a Pentagon plan to ensure the military has access to critical energy, infrastructure and other resources in case of future disruptions.

FEMA quashed any rumors in an X post on Monday, saying, "We've heard a lot of rumors about tomorrow's EAS test. Let's clear things up. It lasts 1 minute, and no action is required. No blackouts, no secret emergencies."

But online speculation continued as the test was being carried out, particularly among social media users who were mistakenly expecting an alert to their phones or didn't understand that the alert wouldn't necessarily occur exactly at 2:20 ET where they were located.

Here's what you need to know about the FEMA test.

Radio and television broadcasters nationwide interrupted their programming with a message that generally said: "This is a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System, issued by the Federal Emergency Management Agency. This is only a test. No action is required by the public."

According to FEMA , the Emergency Alert System involves thousands of independently operated radio, television, cable, satellite and wireline broadband providers. Since they use different equipment, the visual or audio formats may have differed by station.

"The test will include alert tones to support accessibility for individuals who are deaf or hard of hearing," FEMA said before the test was run. And depending on the broadcaster and their capabilities, the message was delivered in English, Spanish or both.

The test wasn't delivered at the exact same time for every American. Because the message had to be carried by "thousands of independently operated radio, television, cable, satellite, and broadband providers," it was received at different times between 2:20 and 2:50 p.m. ET, FEMA said.

TVs and radios that were turned on and tuned to a broadcast station, cable system, satellite radio or television provider, or wireline video service received the test from the EAS, which lasted about one minute.

Why was there a national emergency test?

Federal law requires FEMA to test the Integrated Public Alert and Warning System (IPAWS) at least once every three years. The last national test was conducted on Oct. 4, 2023.

articles.title: NRW taken to court over claims of risk to River Wye and Severn
articles.summary: It follows years of debate over the alleged impacts on rivers in an area dubbed "poultry capital".
articles.body:
River campaigners are taking on Wales' environmental regulator in the High Court over what they believe is a "regulatory gap" that risks pollution from poultry farms in two rivers.

River Action UK has accused Natural Resources Wales (NRW) of not doing enough to assess or address any risk to local rivers and and other water bodies when plans for three farms in Powys were approved last year.

It follows years of debate over the alleged impact of chicken farming on rivers such as the Wye and Severn - in an area dubbed the UK's "poultry capital" .

NRW said it would be inappropriate to comment ahead of the court case, but that it would "participate fully in the legal process".

The case is about plans to increase the capacity of three Powys farms by a combined 336,900 chickens, bringing the total to 522,000.

The three farms are Neuadd Isaf, Rhosddu and Llanshay.

Two of the farms, Rhosddu and Llanshay, are in the River Severn catchment while Neuadd Isaf is in the River Wye catchment.

Campaigners said the Severn was showing "signs of strain" with regular algal blooms, brown algae smothering the riverbed.

Campaigners' concerns have centred around the birds' manure becoming a pollutant when it is spread on fields and leaches into rivers.

Nutrient-rich agricultural run-off can contribute to algal blooms, turning rivers green and smothering wildlife.

Following a consultation, NRW approved permit variations in November 2025, allowing the three poultry units to expand.

Rather than keep and spread the manure on site, the farms' operators said they would export it for use or processing elsewhere.

River Action argued NRW wrongly concluded it had no legal power under the Environmental Permitting Regulations 2016 to assess the potential environmental impacts of this off-site manure management, or to take action to prevent or mitigate pollution arising from it.

Campaigners set up a chicken-themed protest outside the High Court hearing in Llandrindod Wells on Tuesday.

"River Action will argue that Natural Resources Wales has the power to address and assess the impact of that manure on the environment and, as the specialist regulator, should be lawfully deciding how to use that power when operating the permitting regime," said Julia Eriksen, of solicitors Leigh Day, representing River Action.

The organisation insisted NRW could put controls on the farm's permit to reduce or remove the risk of manure causing pollution.

Emma Dearnaley, head of legal at River Action, said NRW "decided that it didn't have the power to look at what would happen when a lot of the manure would go offsite" when the plans were approved last year.

"That matters because more chickens means more muck, and that needs to go somewhere and someone has to deal with it," she said.

"So this case is all about making NRW realise that it does have the power to deal with it."

An NRW spokesperson said: "As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment on matters that are before the court. We will continue to participate fully in the legal process and await the court's determination."

articles.title: U.S. military takes custody of Army officer accused of spying for Russia after U.K. arrest
articles.summary: LONDON — An American Army officer arrested in the United Kingdom on suspicion of spying for Russia has been taken into custody by the U.S. military instead of being charged in Britain, police in London said Tuesday.
articles.body: LONDON — An American Army officer arrested in the United Kingdom on suspicion of spying for Russia has been taken into custody by the U.S. military instead of being charged in Britain, police in London said Tuesday. Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, 41, was arrested Nov. 10 on suspicion of violating the National Security Act by assisting a foreign intelligence service and obtaining or disclosing protected information. The Metropolitan Police said in a news release that “a decision was made to pass the investigation” to American partners. The police say their counterterror force has worked closely with the FBI and U.S. military. “This case should serve as a stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath we all take to protect and defend the Constitution,” U.S. Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, commanding general of the Army’s Counterintelligence Command, said in the release. The Associated Press, citing a U.S. official, has previously reported that Tyner did not hand over any information to the Russians. The Kremlin has denied any connection to the American officer. Tyner, who was previously deployed to Afghanistan, Iraq and Qatar, was a senior human resources officer and had been assigned to a NATO unit at a base near Gloucester, England, about 100 miles west of London. Tyner was serving in NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps at Imjin Barracks near Gloucester. The multinational land unit within the NATO military alliance is designed to quickly respond to crises or short-notice operations. According to the unit’s website, it is made up of forces from 20 nations but is led by the British. Police said the arrest was not related to other counterterrorism investigations, indicating no connection with a suspected terror plot linked to Iran in September at a U.S.-run base in Britain, RAF Fairford, near Gloucester.

articles.body: A military An-12 transport aircraft crashed in Russia’s Kemerovo region in southwestern Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, Russia’s defense ministry was quoted as saying on Tuesday. “The preliminary cause of the disaster is a technical malfunction,” state news agency RIA quoted the Defence Ministry as saying. Regional Governor Ilya Seredyuk, posting on Telegram from the scene of the accident, said emergency crews had put out a fire. articles.title: Gas geyser spews trash and noxious odor into air above L.A. area landfill, prompting public health emergency
articles.summary: Pungent odors wafting from the Chiquita Canyon Landfill prompted Los Angeles County officials to relocate residents after drilling unleashed a geyser of trash and fumes.
articles.body: Pungent odors wafting from the Chiquita Canyon Landfill prompted Los Angeles County officials to order the company responsible to pay to relocate nearby residents after a drilling issue unleashed a geyser of trash and fumes. Members of the fire department responded to the landfill Monday afternoon after a drill released gas into the air. The incident caused a plume of what appeared to be thick black smoke to rise, though it later turned white, according to NBC Los Angeles. A “routine” operation was being done to install a new gas well to help with elevated temperatures, according to a statement Tuesday from Waste Connections, which owns and operates the site. A pressurized pocket within the landfill was affected in the process, it said. “This resulted in an above-ground release of gases and particulate material at the drilling location,” the company said. “No liquids were released, and no injuries have been reported.” Drilling stopped and four people were taken to the hospital for evaluation, but Waste Connections said that no injuries have been reported. The company is conducting air monitoring at the site as well as the local community. There were no indications that there was an excess of chemicals from based on California’s Reference Exposure Levels, the statement said. “Chiquita continues to coordinate with state and local regulatory agencies and emergency response personnel,” Waste Connections said. Los Angeles County’s public health department issued an emergency order Tuesday to have Waste Connections and Chiquita Canyon, LLC, provide immediate relief to the surrounding communities that are exposed to the “noxious odors.” The order instructs the companies to provide residents with indoor spaces meant to provide relief from the odors, to provide short-term hotel stays for the immediate relocation of residents, and transportation for those who require assistance to reach those places. It also ordered that residents be provided support to improve their indoor air quality, such as air filters or purifiers. Chiquita Canyon Landfill “has an obligation to timely and immediately provide relief to mitigate the exposures in the community,” the order said. The work that was being done at the landfill was part of an Environmental Protection Agency order to properly handle the waste and mitigate odors at the landfill. The agency said that the landfill has seen a “significant subsurface elevated temperature event” since around May 2022. The order included directives to redirect offgas by the end of this month. Los Angeles County Supervisor Kathryn Barger described the “explosion and methane plume” as “unacceptable” in a post on X Monday night. “I will be demanding answers and accountability,” Barger wrote.

articles.title: Danny Robins drama The Witch Farm inspired by Brecon 'ghost story'
articles.summary: The "real-life ghost story" of a family who experienced "inexplicable" things is turned into TV drama.
articles.body:
The "real-life ghost story" of a family who experienced "frightening, inexplicable" things after moving to the countryside has been turned into a new TV drama.

The Witch Farm tells the "truly nightmarish" tale of Liz and Bill Rich who left London with their son Jonathan for a remote farmhouse in the foothills of the Brecon Beacons, determined to make a fresh start.

At first the isolation felt like freedom, but the family claimed things began to happen around the house leading them to feel increasingly scared.

Writer and creator, Danny Robins, met Liz who told him "her incredible story", becoming a four part series he beleives will "really surprise people".

Robins, who was also the executive producer of the project, explained how the idea for the four-part series came from a podcast he made for the BBC called The Battersea Poltergeist , which he described as being based on "another real-life ghost story".

"It was a hit around the world and afterwards there was a lot of pressure to find a sequel," he said, which led him to discover the story of Liz and Bill Rich.

In 1989, the young couple moved their family into a remote farmhouse at the foot of a mountain. They claimed to have experienced poltergeist activity, apparitions, alleged possessions and even physical injury.

They say this lasted for seven years and changed them forever, as well as affecting the community around them.

Robins said: "The more I dug into it, the more it felt like something that merited a long-form approach and so we made the podcast series called The Witch Farm .

"Through that process, I met Liz and she told me her incredible story. We also found other witnesses and pieced everything together through a mix of audio drama and documentary.

After finishing the podcast, Robins asked himself "what's next?", admitting that telling the story as a TV documentary "didn't feel right", leading to the decision to dramatise it instead.

Asked what he hopes viewers will feel when they watch the series, Robins said: "I absolutely want people to feel scared, but I also want them to be moved by it.

"It's an incredibly powerful and emotional story, that was one of the things that grabbed me when I first came across it for the podcast."

He also hopes that viewers will "laugh a little", adding that "humour has always been important" to his work.

Robins also hopes to raise the question – 'do ghosts exist?', sparking the debate between belief and scepticism.

"What's crucial for me is that I want viewers to think about it and reach their own conclusions," he said.

The upcoming drama, which was filmed in Wales, stars Port Talbot-born actress Gabrielle Creevy.

She said: "I'm from Wales and I love working here. It's always a pleasure and crews are always so great. I love working in the middle of nowhere in the fresh air - I think I'll always feel the same."

Robins said she brought "absolute authenticity to the role" through her Welsh accent."

Creevy recently featured in the new season of spy thriller Black Doves where she also uses her Welsh accent.

Robins said The Witch Farm is "such a Welsh story", which was considered throughout making the production.

He said an "almost entirely Welsh" crew was used in it's creation, adding: "It's been important that this feels like a story made and told in Wales."

The Witch Farm will be available on BBC iPlayer, BBC One and BBC One Wales from Sunday, 22 November.

articles.title: Russian military plane crash in Siberia kills 19
articles.summary: Russia’s Defence Ministry says preliminary findings for the crash point to equipment failure.
articles.body:
A military plane has crashed in western Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, according to a statement from the Russian Defence Ministry, cited by local media.

The Antonov An-12 transport aircraft went down in an unpopulated area near the city of Kemerovo, about 3,000km east of Moscow. The An-12 typically has a crew of six.

Air force experts were investigating the cause of the crash, but preliminary findings pointed to equipment failure.

“A commission from the Russian Aerospace Forces is working at the site to establish all the circumstances of the incident,” the ministry’s statement was quoted as saying by the RIA Novosti news agency.

Regional Governor Ilya Seredyuk, posting on Telegram from the scene of the accident, said emergency crews had extinguished a fire. He said crews were helping to investigate the accident.

Seredyuk, in a video posted online showing the site of the accident near the village of Yagunovo, said the plane had been flying through the region when it crashed.

The Investigative Committee, Russia’s top criminal investigation agency, launched an inquiry into possible violations of flight safety rules, a standard practice following crashes.

The An-12 is a Soviet-built four-engine turboprop transport plane that has been in service since the late 1950s. More than 1,000 were built, and some still remain in operation in Russia and other nations.

In September, a Russian Tupolev Tu-95 military aircraft crashed in the eastern region of Amur, killing six crew members and injuring a seventh.
